item.title: What to Watch in Virginia’s First Primary Since Its Redistricting Battle
item.description:
Democrats across the country celebrated in April after Virginia voters greenlit a plan to cut the number of safe Republican House seats in the state from five to just one. Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House minority leader, said he hoped that the new congressional map would offset the Republican Party’s gains in states including Texas, North Carolina, Ohio and Missouri, which drew new district lines at President Trump’s behest.

But the Democrats’ new congressional map dissolved just weeks later, when the Virginia Supreme Court ruled it was unconstitutional. The decision sunk Democrats’ nearly $70 million investment in the referendum and plunged hopefuls into another round of of musical chairs: Some candidates dropped out of races that had once seemed winnable, and others returned to hostile territory.

Virginia Democrats are still bullish, saying they expect to flip at least two seats this cycle. Here are some of the major races in the state as voters head to the polls for Tuesday’s primary, the first election since the congressional maps were passed.

Before the old map was restored, Representative Rob Wittman, a Republican, was facing a re-election campaign in a Richmond-area district that Vice President Kamala Harris would have carried by seven points in 2024. Instead, Mr. Wittman is now the nominee in a district along the state’s eastern flank that Mr. Trump carried by five percentage points that year.

But Democrats still see the seat as one of their best opportunities for a flip in November. The House Democratic campaign arm has supported Shannon Taylor, a prosecutor running on a law-and-order platform. Ms. Taylor has raised more than $2.1 million so far, significantly more than any of her six opponents.

In 2022, bipartisan redistricting helped Representative Jen Kiggans, a Navy veteran and a Republican, oust the incumbent, Elaine Luria, in Virginia’s Second Congressional District.

Now, Ms. Kiggans is likely to face a high-stakes rematch in a seat that the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated as one of the nation’s 18 most competitive districts. Ms. Luria, who is also a Navy veteran, is the front-runner among the four candidates competing for the Democratic nomination for the district. Ms. Luria has the backing of the Democratic establishment.

Former Representative Tom Perriello, a Democrat, jumped into the primary for a largely rural central Virginia district when the proposed map promised friendly terrain. Mr. Perriello leads the field of three Democrats, but with the old boundaries restored, the winner faces a steep challenge in the general election in a district Mr. Trump carried by 12 points in 2024.

Representative John McGuire, a former Navy SEAL elected in 2024, is under pressure in the Republican primary from Melanie Lucero, a real estate broker and Marine veteran who has cast Mr. McGuire as a “career politician” who is out of touch with constituents.

An architect of the redistricting push, Dan Helmer, a Democratic House delegate, opened a congressional run this year for a seat redrawn to lean heavily blue. But he dropped out after the state Supreme Court decision pulled it back to safely Republican territory.

Beth Macy, the author of the popular nonfiction book “Dopesick” on the opioid epidemic in Appalachia, was set to run in a district that Kamala Harris would have carried by eight points in 2024. Representative Ben Cline, a Republican, regained a glide path to victory in the district in May, but Ms. Macy has stayed in the race, telling The New York Times that Democrats “can’t just roll over.”

Unopposed in his primary, Senator Mark Warner, 71, is locked in for a final re-election bid. Mr. Warner, the influential vice chair of both the Senate Democratic Caucus and the Senate Intelligence Committee, is heavily favored to win a fourth term, giving Democrats what they hope will be a boost in voter turnout. He was first elected in 2008.

item.title: A D.S.A. Member Aims for a Comeback: What to Watch in Missouri’s Primaries
item.description:
Missouri voters will decide a consequential slate of primary contests and constitutional ballot measures on Tuesday.

The results could not only reshape the state’s tax structure and its process for amending its constitution, but also serve as a litmus test for the national Democratic Party’s ideological divide.

Here’s what to watch.

The marquee primary on Tuesday is a fiery rematch in Missouri’s First Congressional District, where Representative Wesley Bell, a moderate first-term Democrat, faces off against former Representative Cori Bush, a progressive member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

In 2024, Mr. Bell — a former prosecutor and member of the Ferguson, Mo., City Council — ousted Ms. Bush, a former Black Lives Matter organizer who was part of a progressive group of congresswomen known as “the squad.” Two years later, Ms. Bush, who represented the St. Louis area for two terms, is attempting a comeback in a race that highlights the rift between the Democratic Party’s moderate and progressive wings.

Mr. Bell has maintained a distinct fund-raising advantage, and holds key endorsements from House Democratic leadership, including Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, and the Congressional Black Caucus PAC. Ms. Bush has the backing of Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and the Democratic Socialists of America.

Ms. Bush has anchored her campaign on vocal opposition to the war in Gaza and criticism of pro-Israel groups, betting that Democrats have further soured on Israel since she was voted out in 2024.

The United Democracy Project, the main super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, has poured more than $3 million into advertising opposing Ms. Bush’s bid this cycle, a repeat of its heavy spending against her in 2024.

Missourians are voting on whether to require that citizen-initiated constitutional amendments must win in each of the state’s eight congressional districts, rather than by a simple statewide majority.

The measure, backed by Republicans, would make it significantly harder to pass even popular changes to the state’s founding document, given the widely differing ideological makeups of each district.

Missourians have used citizen-initiated amendments to enshrine the right to abortion, expand access to free health insurance and legalize marijuana and sports betting. None of those would have passed under the new standard, which was proposed by the Republican-led legislature.

If the measure passes, constitutional amendments proposed by the legislature would continue to require only a simple majority, or more than 50 percent of the vote. This would make Missouri the only state whose processes for passing citizen-led and legislature-led ballot initiatives are different.

In fiscal year 2025, money from individual income taxes made up more than 60 percent of the state’s general revenue.

A proposed constitutional amendment would instruct the legislature to phase out those taxes, a drastic overhaul of the state budget. The measure would authorize lawmakers to drive up sales taxes to replace the lost revenue, but it does not specify how that should be done.

The state’s governor, Mike Kehoe, a Republican, says the move would catalyze economic growth. But opponents say it would increase taxes for lower-income Missourians.

If it passes, the measure would make Missouri the 10th state in the country to exclude income taxes as a revenue source.

item.title: Republicans Try to Flip a Governor’s Mansion: What to Watch in Kansas’ Primaries
item.description:
Primary elections on Tuesday in Kansas will center on the race for the open governor’s mansion, a judicial ballot measure with consequences for abortion and L.G.B.T.Q. rights, and high-profile intraparty battles for both the U.S. House and Senate.

Here’s what to watch:

In Kansas, all eyes are on the primaries for the marquee governor’s race, which Republicans see as perhaps their best chance this year to flip a governorship held by Democrats.

President Trump has endorsed Ty Masterson, the president of the State Senate. But Philip Sarnecki, a businessman, and Scott Schwab, the Kansas secretary of state, are also looking to win over conservative primary voters, and Vicki Schmidt, the state insurance commissioner, has staked out a moderate lane.

Democratic primary voters have a choice of three experienced politicians, all from suburban Kansas City. State Senator Ethan Corson was endorsed by Gov. Laura Kelly, a moderate Democrat who was barred by term limits from running again. Mr. Corson faces State Senator Cindy Holscher, who called for a moratorium on data centers, and Mayor Curt Skoog of Overland Park.

Kansas primary voters will also weigh in on a ballot measure that would overhaul the way State Supreme Court justices are selected. Anti-abortion groups and other socially conservative organizations are supporting the measure.

If it succeeds, the seven justices would be elected, rather than being appointed by the governor and standing periodically for retention votes. (All but one of the justices on the court were appointed by a Democratic governor.)

The measure is, in part, a response to a 2019 Kansas Supreme Court decision that recognized a right to abortion, which voters in the state declined to overturn in 2022.

In Kansas, 11 Democrats are vying for the nomination to challenge Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, who is expected to win his two-way G.O.P. primary and has stockpiled more than $5.3 million for the general election.

Recent polls and fund-raising numbers have so far indicated that Adam Hamilton, a well-known pastor who has positioned himself as a moderate, is leading the Democratic primary field.

Whoever wins the primary will face a steep uphill battle. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, giving the state the nation’s longest streak of electing Republican senators. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 16 percentage points against Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

Representative Sharice Davids, a fourth-term member of Congress who holds Kansas’ lone Democratic seat, is facing a primary challenge from Sarah Preu, a progressive technology industry professional. Ms. Preu has said she would vote to defund Immigration and Customs Enforcement, “end forever wars” and stop sending U.S. arms to Israel.

On the Republican side, Chase LaPorte, an Army veteran and business administrator, is the only candidate who has reported raising money.

Ms. Davids, who was one of the first two Native American women to win election to Congress in history, won by more than 10 points in 2024. The seat will be considered competitive in November, but Democrats would be facing far longer odds there if the State Legislature had gone forward with a redistricting plan pushed by Mr. Trump.

item.title: Blanche Clears Crucial Vote, Nearing Confirmation as Attorney General
item.description:
Todd Blanche, whose role in a much-criticized deal to resolve President Trump’s lawsuit against the I.R.S. nearly scuttled his confirmation as attorney general, cleared a crucial hurdle on Tuesday after the Senate Judiciary Committee narrowly approved his nomination.

After a week of uncertainty, Mr. Blanche was confirmed by a 12-to-10 vote along party lines, exemplifying a widening schism over the direction of a department at the center of Mr. Trump’s effort to punish and humiliate his perceived enemies.

Mr. Blanche, the president’s former defense lawyer and the acting attorney general, broke an impasse over his confirmation after he reached an agreement with two Republican holdouts on the committee late Sunday. Mr. Blanche released written assurances that he would kill a proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund that could have been used to pay Jan. 6 rioters and limit the scope of a deal granting broad tax immunity to Mr. Trump and his family.

Mr. Blanche’s nomination now advances to the Senate floor, with a vote possible as early as this week. It was not immediately clear whether he would be confirmed, given that several Republicans have yet to commit to supporting him and that he can afford to lose only two senators on a party-line vote because of Senator Mitch McConnell’s continued absence.

Two lame-duck Republicans, Senator John Cornyn of Texas and Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, voted with their party’s majority on the committee after briefly defying the White House over concerns about the highly unusual fund and a tax immunity deal that could save the president $100 million.

Former department officials have said that Mr. Blanche’s written assurances can be easily reversed, or evaded. The department has broad authority to dispense cash to Mr. Trump’s allies through existing department processes. Tax experts said that the new limits on his immunity agreement did nothing to keep Mr. Trump and his family from an enormous windfall offered to no other taxpayers.

Mr. Cornyn acknowledged on Tuesday that the concessions offered in exchange for his vote could be reversed by Mr. Trump but said he hoped that Mr. Blanche would hold the line. He called Mr. Blanche a “stabilizing force” in the department who had earned enough trust with the president to tell him “hard truths,” even if he was ignored.

He concluded with a plea, asking Mr. Blanche “not to be afraid to capitalize on that earned trust when necessary for the good of the country.”

The committee vote represents a de facto endorsement by Senate Republicans of Mr. Blanche’s actions in running the day-to-day operations of a Justice Department that has surrendered much of its independence to the White House on his watch.

Republicans like Mr. Cornyn have been willing to put aside their deep concerns about Mr. Blanche’s lack of independence for the sake of partisan comity. They also see him as the best choice they could possibly get from a White House whose first pick, in November 2024, was Matt Gaetz, the former Florida congressman who had once been accused of sex trafficking.

Incensed Democrats, speaking before the vote took place, said that committee Republicans had frittered away their one chance to reassert independence and rule of law at the department — and constrained their objections to narrow questions while ignoring whether Mr. Blanche was fit to serve.

“Instead of serving the American people and upholding the rule of law and the Constitution, Mr. Blanche has aided and abetted the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States,” said Senator Richard J. Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the committee.

Mr. Durbin accused Mr. Blanche of perjuring himself by denying during his confirmation hearing that he had told Mr. Durbin and his staff that creating the fund was a “mistake” during a private meeting.

“What’s left of this committee?” asked Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat.

Mr. Tillis raised a new issue as he explained Mr. Blanche’s vote — the department’s sign-off on the indictment of James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director, on widely ridiculed charges that a photograph Mr. Comey posted of seashells on a beach arrayed with a message threatened Mr. Trump.

“What I hope I see out of him is a bending of the curve of this absurdity,” he said.

He went on to accuse Democrats, under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., of initiating politically motivated investigations but conceded that the weaponization of the department was “a little bit more intense in this administration than the last one.”

For the first time, Senator Charles E. Grassley, the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, publicly endorsed the push by Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis, saying he believed that it was “a crime” that it took so long for the White House and Justice Department to put the changes in writing.

Mr. Grassley, a reliable wingman for the White House, had not expressed any of those concerns previously. But on Tuesday, he said skepticism about the deal was “shared by many, including this senator,” and thanked Mr. Blanche and the White House for putting “this issue to bed once and for all.”

Mr. Blanche, who has maintained that Mr. Trump has a nearly unfettered right to dictate prosecutorial, personnel and policy decisions under Article II of the Constitution, has overseen a wholesale transformation of the department.

He has supervised the dismissals or forced transfers of experienced career lawyers, the abandonment of investigations into Mr. Trump’s political allies and a nearly nonstop succession of actions against his enemies, including the recent indictment of Mr. Comey.

Democrats said that the frenetic final negotiations that led to Mr. Blanche’s victory in the committee — including Mr. Trump’s threat to temporarily withdraw Mr. Blanche’s nomination rather than give up the fund or surrender his tax benefit — proved that he was unwilling to stand up to the president.

Hours after the committee vote, Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, voiced skepticism about Mr. Blanche, saying she did not intend to back him when his confirmation reached the Senate floor.

Ms. Collins, who is running for re-election in a state that Republicans lost in 2024, said in a statement that he had “taken several actions that have further eroded” the Justice Department’s independence. She cited the settlement that Mr. Blanche negotiated in Mr. Trump’s lawsuit against the I.R.S., including his approval of the so-called weaponization fund.

Two other Republican senators have expressed concerns about Mr. Blanche’s nomination and have not committed to supporting him.

Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska told reporters this week that she wanted to have further conversations with Mr. Blanche. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who lost his re-election bid to a primary challenger backed by Mr. Trump, has said he is concerned that the Justice Department may be targeting the president’s political opponents.

Mr. Cassidy has pointed in recent days to an investigation of Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide who testified before Congress about the attack at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

item.title: An Invasive Mosquito Is Spreading With Alarming Speed, Threatening Africa’s Cities
item.description:
An invasive, malaria-carrying, insecticide-resistant mosquito that thrives in cities, where malaria has not been a major threat, has moved farther and faster across Africa than even pessimistic scientists had feared. And many public health experts believe it is too late to eliminate, or even contain, it.

A new genomic analysis of the mosquito, called Anopheles stephensi, using specimens collected from 10 countries, showed that those found in Africa had genetic resistance to all of the chemicals currently used in spraying campaigns and other mosquito-control efforts, meaning those insecticides will not kill it.

It is moving with terrifying efficiency and speed across flat, open, windy terrain, pushing westward to Ghana and south through Kenya, from its initial arrival on the continent in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa more than a decade ago.

“The last couple of years there’s less talk of, ‘We really need to contain this invasion,’ because everyone who knows what’s what realizes that genie is completely out of the bottle,” said Tristan Dennis, who studies vector genomics at the University of Queensland in Australia and who led the new analysis, published in the journal Science.

This mosquito alarms health experts because, unlike the species that historically spread malaria in Africa, it thrives in urban as well as rural areas, and is not deterred by dry seasons. This means that malaria, already one of the top killers in Africa, could become a grave problem in megacities such as Lagos and Kinshasa, each of which are home to about 20 million people.

“We’ve not had to worry about malaria in urban settings,” said Dr. Eric Ochomo, the head of entomology for the Kenya Medical Research Institute.

Much of the urban population has no immunity to malaria, and the parasite will make people gravely ill, he said. And when a stable population of stephensi is established, it transmits malaria all year, not just on the rainy season cycle most current malaria programs are structured to address.

“It’s going to really complicate our ability to manage malaria,” Dr. Ochomo said.

In most countries, stephensi is not yet established in populations big enough to detect whether it is affecting malaria rates. But in Djibouti and Ethiopia, the first countries it invaded, it is possible to see the risk it represents.

Before stephensi arrived in 2013, Djibouti was on the cusp of declaring malaria eradicated. In 2012, there were just 27 cases. A year after stephensi was found, cases shot up to nearly 1,700. Each year thereafter, the number crept up, and in 2020, there was an explosion: more than 70,000 cases.

In Dire Dawa, Ethiopia’s second-largest city, stephensi drove a surge of malaria cases in 2022, one that initially baffled health care workers who were not used to diagnosing or treating the disease.

The spread of stephensi is yet another setback in an already sputtering battle with mosquitoes in Africa. In 2024, there were nine million more malaria cases than in 2023. While the full 2025 data is not available yet, and will be less comprehensive due to health program funding cuts, there are clear signs that malaria is resurgent.

Teams of scientists have been working together, often against a backdrop of armed conflict and climate-driven displacement, to combine their bare-bones surveillance efforts and map the dimensions of the new threat.

Mahaman Lamine, a parasitologist in the city of Zinder in the West African nation Niger, trapped a pile of mosquitoes around ponds with a couple of students in 2024. In his university lab, he asked the students to identify the species for a biodiversity survey, and almost as an afterthought reminded them about stephensi, the invasive species that had been detected elsewhere in Africa. A short while later, his students mentioned that they had found some of those in their samples.

“I said, ‘No, no, no!’” Dr. Lamine recalled.

Stephensi had never been found in Niger. But Dr. Lamine rechecked the mosquitoes against one morphological key, and then another. They matched. Soon he dispatched a student on a bus to the city of Kano, across the border in Nigeria, carrying mosquito samples through an area with an armed insurgency to reach a lab that could do molecular confirmation.

The students were right: Anopheles stephensi had reached Niger.

The recently published genomic analysis showed that after arriving in Djibouti, the new African stephensi population split into three groups. One went into Ethiopia, then south into Kenya; one skipped from Djibouti over a narrow channel in the Red Sea and into Yemen; and one went into Sudan and from there headed east across the Sahel to West Africa.

Other scientists have speculated that stephensi has been introduced from South Asia via ports in West Africa in separate incidents, but the genomic analysis provided a compelling case for how efficiently the mosquito had moved across the flat, windy Sahel, expanding its territory by as much as about 300 miles a year.

“We’ve never seen anything like this, this kind of spread. We never imagined a mosquito could spread this fast,” said Dr. Ochomo, who contributed mosquito samples to the study.

A few years ago, he expected stephensi to pose a threat only in Kenya’s very dry north. It has already been found moving steadily south and fanning out through different kinds of habitats.

Stephensi arrived in Africa in about 2013, likely on a ship from Pakistan or India. Researchers in Djibouti identified it as they were scrambling to explain a massive spike in malaria cases in a country that had been on the verge of eradicating the disease.

Everywhere it goes, stephensi encounters malaria-control programs trying to do more with shrinking budgets. The United States, the world’s largest funder of anti-malaria efforts, slashed its support at the start of the Trump administration. Malaria-control budgets were reduced by a third or more in most countries with a high malaria prevalence last year, compared to 2024.

“The first thing cut is surveillance,” Dr. Ochomo said. Yet without data on which mosquito is where, it is harder to make decisions about where to invest in interventions, such as bed net distribution. “If we could do really good surveillance, we could decide where to put the limited resources,” he said.

In Niger, Dr. Lamine is also struggling to continue to track the mosquito. “We do not have any funding, and we have only one very old microscope. But we try to do the work, because we love science,” he said.

Dr. Dennis said stephensi was benefiting from human interaction with the environment.

“They’ve come at a time when there’s massive fragility and instability, lots of displaced people, very little state control in some places, on a really rapidly urbanizing continent,” he said. “And they came armed to the teeth with defenses against the insecticides we can use.”

Scientists fear that stephensi has also reached other countries, including Chad, Somalia, Eritrea and South Sudan, nations that do not have the resources for national vector surveillance. “Nobody is looking,” Dr. Dennis said.

Scientists in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Iran, the United States and Saudi Arabia collaborated to do the genomic study, to home in on where the African stephensi population originated. Almoevery country had violent conflicts raging when the research began or descended into war over the four years of the work.

Hmooda Toto Kafy, a medical entomologist with the ministry of health in Sudan, contributed samples from his country, collecting the last of them just weeks before the civil war began. Dr. Kafy has been poised to start research on if and how stephensi is driving malaria transmission in the country. “But this is not easily done during the war,” he said.

Regions he hoped his team could surveil are inaccessible because of fighting, while staff members and students left as refugees. And the banking system is in disarray, so it is difficult to pay for supplies. All of it makes the already daunting prospect of hunting for a tiny mosquito in one of the world’s largest countries massively more complex.

In Yemen, Dr. Tarek Sultan Bin Hawail, a public health specialist, supervised a team that collected samples for the study, and shared ominous findings with researchers in Africa. His team found stephensi in the huge camps that ring the Yemeni capital Aden, housing people displaced by the country’s civil war. There were mosquito larvae in the water containers inside people’s homes and tents — living alongside another mosquito, Aedes aegypti, which carries dengue fever and other viruses.

Health workers at clinics overwhelmed with patients with fevers were treating patients with dengue, because malaria was not supposed to be in the area. Stephensi brought it.

Africa is home to nearly half the global total of displaced people; there are 15 million displaced by the war in Sudan alone.

When the global network of scientists had contributed samples, Dr. Dennis carried out the genomic analysis. His findings were bleak. “All of the resistance genes in the invasive population confer resistance to pretty much every insecticide we are using in vector control, so this is actually even worse news than we thought it was,” Dr. Dennis said.

Even with the growing body of evidence about how stephensi is moving and where, there are few signs of resources being shifted to meet it. “You can have these data that tell you a certain thing, but if there’s not the infrastructure to put a response into practice, then it doesn’t help much,” said Dr. Dennis.

Despite this, the scientists who study stephensi speak about the mosquito with grudging admiration.

Typically an invasive species struggles to establish itself in a new place, shrinking down to a small population with limited genetic diversity.

“The fact that this mosquito was able to lose a huge amount of genetic diversity and then still go on to occupy this vast swath of the continent,” Dr. Dennis said. “It took over Africa.”

item.title: Gluesenkamp Perez Faces a Challenge: What to Watch in Washington State’s Primaries
item.description:
Washington State’s primary elections on Tuesday offer a significant test of political polarization and President Trump’s influence.

In the Third Congressional District, Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez — a moderate Democrat who has regularly broken with her party to work across the aisle — is fighting off challengers from both the right and left to defend a rural swing district that voted three times for Mr. Trump. At the same time, in the conservative Fourth District in Central Washington, the retirement of Representative Dan Newhouse, a Republican, has touched off a scramble among G.O.P. contenders.

Under Washington’s nonpartisan primary system, all candidates appear on a single ballot regardless of party affiliation, with only the top two vote-getters advancing to the general election. Washington and California are the only states that use a nonpartisan “top-two” primary mechanism in congressional races.

Here’s what to watch:

Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez’s seat is one of just 18 rated as tossups by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, and is a top target for Republicans.

Mr. Trump has backed John Braun, the minority leader of the Washington State Senate and a retired Navy captain, betting that he is the best Republican to unseat Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez. Mr. Braun owns a business that manufactures emergency vehicles, and has campaigned heavily on economic issues.

Ms. Gluesenkamp Perez, a former co-owner of an auto shop who has sought to appeal to blue-collar voters, is also facing a serious challenge from Brent Hennrich, a progressive. But she is expected to advance to the general election.

In total, three Republicans, four Democrats, one independent and one member of the Cascade Party — a minor, centrist political party founded by the former Nirvana bassist Krist Novoselic — are running in the nonpartisan primary in the Third Congressional District, which touches the Pacific Ocean and the Oregon border.

Mr. Newhouse’s retirement has opened his safely red seat in Central Washington for new blood after his more than 10 years in office. He was one of 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach the president after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol, putting him at odds with Mr. Trump.

Whoever replaces him is likely to be much more aligned with the president: Both Republicans running have courted Mr. Trump’s endorsement. The president is backing Amanda McKinney, a Yakima County commissioner, over Jerrod Sessler, an entrepreneur and former NASCAR driver who has run unsuccessfully in previous cycles.

item.title: What to Watch in Michigan’s High-Stakes Primary Elections
item.description:
See the latest results in today’s key races including updates on the Michigan Senate primary, plus more elections in Michigan, Missouri, Kansas, Virginia and Washington.

Voters in Michigan are heading to the polls on Tuesday to decide a bruising, high-stakes Democratic Senate primary and closely-watched Democratic House races that could offer clues about the party’s direction.

Here’s what to know about Primary Day in Michigan, a perennial swing state.

The Democratic Senate primary pits two candidates with starkly different visions for their party.

The winner will try to protect a seat that the retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters is vacating. The general-election race is expected to be one of the most competitive contests in the country in November.

In the Democratic primary, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, has staged a freewheeling campaign centered on his opposition to American aid for Israel and his support for universal health care.

He says the moment calls for systemic change. His supporters say he is channeling the hopes of rank-and-file Democrats.

He faces Representative Haley Stevens, a centrist who is strongly supportive of Israel, backs more modest health care reforms and says she wants to rein in ICE, but not eliminate it.

She says the moment calls for elected officials who will work to make Washington more functional. Her supporters say she would be a stronger general-election candidate.

In the Republican primary, former Representative Mike Rogers is running unopposed.

An unusually large number of incumbents have lost in Democratic House primaries this year, as left-wing energy has lifted a series of insurgents.

Progressives hope another incumbent, Representative Shri Thanedar of Detroit, will fall Tuesday. But Mr. Thanedar’s race against State Representative Donavan McKinney, a democratic socialist, isn’t simply a proxy battle between moderates and progressives.

It’s also a messy fight that has touched on racial identity. Mr. Thanedar is Indian American, and since he won his seat in 2022, Detroit, a majority Black city, has not had a Black representative in Washington.

Some Black leaders, including five members of the Congressional Black Caucus, have rallied behind Mr. McKinney, who is Black. They have broken with Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the leader of House Democrats, who is Black and has endorsed Mr. Thanedar.

In an interview, Mr. McKinney said Detroit voters were focused less on racial identity than on whether the district would have a “pro-working-class agenda.”

Democrats are hoping to unseat Representative Tom Barrett, a first-term Republican who serves a battleground district anchored by Lansing, the state capital, and nearby Michigan State University.

But Democrats must first pick a nominee. And the primary has been bruising.

Voters are choosing between two moderate Democrats — Bridget Brink, a diplomat in the Biden and Trump administrations, and Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL endorsed by Senator Elissa Slotkin — and a progressive activist, William Lawrence, who is supported by Senator Bernie Sanders and has campaigned with Dr. El-Sayed.

Mr. Barrett, who is considered one of the country’s most endangered Republican incumbents, has sought to separate himself from President Trump, joining Democrats who voted to direct the president to end the war with Iran or seek explicit authorization to continue it.

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a term-limited Democrat, is set to leave office at the end of the year.

Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, is expected to win the Democratic nomination on Tuesday in the race to replace Ms. Whitmer.

In the general election, Ms. Benson, the state’s top election official, may face Representative John James, a Trump-endorsed Republican from a swing suburban Detroit district, who said at a rally with President Trump last month that the president had won Michigan three times. Mr. Trump did not. (He won it twice, carrying it in 2016 and 2024, but losing it by more than 100,000 votes in 2020.)

Mr. James has led Perry Johnson, a businessman, in polls of the Republican primary. Mr. Johnson has also echoed Mr. Trump’s election falsehoods. He said in an interview that Mr. Trump “of course” won the general election in 2020.

item.title: An Angry Trump Struggles to Understand Iran’s Defiant Leaders
item.description:
President Trump’s angry claim on Monday that Iran was being “unbelievably duplicitous” in its dealings with the United States was just the latest sign of his struggle to understand his rivals in Tehran.

Mr. Trump considers himself a master of sizing up and exploiting his adversaries. But Iran’s leaders have baffled him.

“All they do is make me angry,” he told reporters last week. “They just make me angry.”

More frustration could be in store for the American president. Trump officials say a new deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz may be near, but Iran continues to insist on collecting fees there that Mr. Trump has ruled unacceptable.

Mr. Trump’s inability to strike a favorable deal with Iran has not only cost him politically among war-weary voters, but continued strife around the crucial waterway has made for volatile oil prices at the expense of American consumers and the global economy.

Mr. Trump is hardly the first U.S. president who has struggled to read Iran. Each of his predecessors since the country’s 1979 Islamic Revolution has tried to decode Iran’s murky power structure and the mind-set of its political leadership.

Most have come up short; some have been burned badly. A rare exception is President Barack Obama, whose 2015 nuclear deal with Iran was a 20-month diplomatic effort. Mr. Obama considered it a major achievement, despite criticism from Republicans and some Democrats that Iran had lured him into a flawed deal by feigning moderation.

But Mr. Trump may be the president who “has least understood Iran’s leadership,” said Kenneth Pollack, a former C.I.A. analyst and National Security Council official who has studied Iran for decades.

“In many ways, Trump represents the epitome of America’s frustrations with Iran,” Mr. Pollack said. “He has been both the most desirous of making a deal with Iran, and the one who used the most force against it. He has found that neither got him what he wanted.”

Mr. Trump often speaks as though massive force will produce a quick deal.

After the war opened with a Feb. 28 airstrike that killed Iran’s supreme leader of nearly 40 years, Ali Khamenei, Mr. Trump called on Iran’s people to rise up and “take over” their government. He added that he would then “choose” Iran’s next leader.

More senior Iranian officials would also be killed in airstrikes. But no popular uprising emerged.

Iran’s hard-line government instead doubled down. In March, it named a new supreme leader, Mr. Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba Khamenei. U.S. officials consider him even more rigid — and more interested in acquiring a nuclear bomb — than his father.

Iran had simply ignored Mr. Trump’s public declaration that the younger Mr. Khamenei would be an “unacceptable” choice. And Mr. Khamenei did not respond to a public offer from Mr. Trump for an in-person meeting.

Even so, Mr. Trump retained hope for major change. “Iran can get themselves on a very good footing if they make a deal,” he said in late April. Iran, he said, could become “a legitimate country, not a country based on death and horror.”

Iranian officials say they can negotiate with Mr. Trump on matters such as the Strait of Hormuz and their nuclear program, even as they rule out many of his core demands.

But in a political system premised on hatred of the United States, none show interest in a larger reconciliation with the United States.

There are few signs that Mr. Trump’s months of dealing with Iran’s regime have given him a clearer understanding of it. Over the course of the conflict, Mr. Trump has constantly revised his assessment of Mr. Khamenei and his deputies. He has branded them “lunatics,” “reasonable,” “crazy bastards,” “very smart” and “stone cold crazy.”

Mr. Trump is to some degree experiencing frustrations that have bedeviled several of his predecessors who also hoped for grand bargains with Iran.

“For decades, American policymakers have consistently underappreciated the ideological commitment and deeply institutionalized structure of power in the Islamic Republic,” said Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director for foreign policy at the Brookings Institution in Washington.

One problem, Maloney noted, is how little direct exposure U.S. officials have had to top Iranian leaders. No U.S. official ever met Iran’s first supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, or the late Mr. Khamenei, nor his son.

Ms. Maloney said that war appears to have strengthened the power of Iran’s religious and military leadership, leaving no “viable alternative power center.”

Iran’s semi-democratic political system, which features a president and parliament under the total religious authority of its supreme leader, has at times included high-level officials open to friendlier relations with the United States.

But past appeals by Washington to those figures have mostly ended in regret.

Dennis Ross, a veteran of Middle East diplomacy who served presidents of both parties, said that “the Iranians seem to understand us better than we understand them.”

In 1980, President Jimmy Carter approved secret talks with Iran’s foreign minister in an effort to free the 52 American hostages seized from the U.S. Embassy in Tehran the year before.

Mr. Carter’s diary entries show him obsessing, much like Mr. Trump, on details of Iran’s political machinations — including feuds among top Iranian officials.

In early 1980 Mr. Carter thought he had struck a deal to free the hostages in return for the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets and a pledge of American noninterference in Iranian affairs, among other things.

But in what Mr. Carter called “a bitter disappointment,” Mr. Khomeini shot down the idea, blindsiding American officials and his own subordinates. Mr. Carter would eventually order a hostage rescue mission that failed before finalizing a deal that freed the Americans on his last day in office.

Five years later, President Ronald Reagan directed aides to explore a message from an Iranian arms dealer who claimed that moderate Iranian officials would be open to establishing friendly ties once the aging Mr. Khomeini had died.

In what Mr. Reagan later called a search for “a strategic opening,” he approved the secret sale of U.S. weapons to Iran in exchange for the release of American hostages held in Lebanon. The arrangement became part of what is known as the Iran-contra affair because money from the arms sales was covertly diverted, in defiance of Congress, to an anti-communist rebel group in Nicaragua known as the contras.

The affair’s exposure engulfed Mr. Reagan’s presidency in scandal, as several U.S. officials pleaded guilty or were convicted of felonies; Mr. Reagan’s former national security adviser attempted suicide.

The opening with Iran turned out to be a mirage. No friendly moderates emerged in Tehran, and the C.I.A. believed the arms dealer who began it all was a fraud. Mr. Reagan, denying knowledge of key events, apologized in a national address, while defending his original goal of courting Iranian moderates.

A more tangible opportunity emerged for President Bill Clinton in 1997, when Iran elected a reformist candidate, Mohammad Khatami, as its president. Mr. Khatami called for good relations with the United States, and even expressed regret for the embassy hostage crisis.

This was the real thing.

Mr. Clinton reciprocated with gestures such as the restoration of U.S. imports of Iranian pistachios and carpets, and conciliatory remarks acknowledging some of Iran’s historical grievances.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright even issued a public apology for the C.I.A.’s backing of a 1953 coup that overthrew Iran’s prime minister after he nationalized the country’s Western-dominated oil industry.

But powerful hard-liners opposed Mr. Khatami’s moderate vision, in part because reconciliation with the United States threatened the foundations of their anti-Western ideology.

Days after Ms. Albright’s speech, the elder Mr. Khamenei, who became supreme leader after Mr. Khomeini’s death in 1989, dismissed her words — and any possibility of dialogue with Washington.

Mr. Khatami later said privately that Mr. Khamenei believed that Iran could never make peace with the United States, according to Karim Sadjadpour, an Iran expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Only Mr. Obama has pulled off a major diplomatic agreement with Iran, in the form of the 2015 nuclear deal that placed limits on Iran’s atomic program lasting up to 15 years in exchange for relief from economic sanctions.

Many officials in the Obama administration hoped that agreement, negotiated with another moderate Iranian leader, Hassan Rouhani, might be a first step toward better relations. But that was not to be. Mr. Khamenei approved the deal, but showed no desire for taking things further; critics said that confirmed their warnings that Mr. Rouhani would amount to a replay of Mr. Khatami.

Iranian suspicions that the U.S. could not be trusted were soon affirmed. In 2018, Mr. Trump withdrew from the nuclear deal and imposed even harsher economic sanctions than had been in place before the agreement.

Iran responded by accelerating its nuclear program, putting it on course for a violent collision with the United States and the war Mr. Trump initiated in February.

Since then, Mr. Ross said, Iran has continued to outmaneuver Washington, which Mr. Trump’s obvious impatience to conclude the war has made easier.

“They tend to read our sense of urgency as a form of leverage,” Mr. Ross said. “We always seem in a hurry to get things done. They operate under the premise that time serves their interests more than ours.”

item.title: Shrugging Off Trump’s Warning, Max Miller Pushes Ahead in Ohio
item.description:
When President Trump called Representative Max Miller, his former loyal aide, to warn him the domestic abuse allegations he was facing would make it tough for him to win re-election, Republican officials at the White House and in Ohio hoped it would be enough to get the embattled congressman to drop out.

But Mr. Trump stopped short of asking Mr. Miller to step aside, and the congressman made it clear he had no intention of doing so, according to two people familiar with the call who spoke about the confidential conversation on the condition of anonymity.

The president, who endorsed Mr. Miller in May, has yet to publicly withdraw his support, leaving other Republicans reluctant to do so themselves.

The exchange, which was reported earlier by Axios, has left the G.O.P. in a bind as officials scramble to figure out how to protect a House seat that the party cannot afford to lose in the midterm elections, with a headstrong candidate and a fast-approaching deadline to get him out of the race.

If Mr. Miller were to drop out by the end of the day on Tuesday, there would be a special primary election to replace him on the ballot. Otherwise, Ohio law suggests he would need to resign by Friday to trigger a meeting of state party chairs, who would have to choose a new candidate by Monday.

The tight time frame has transformed what up until recently had been a family feud between two of the state’s most powerful families into a political crisis that has forced Republican officials to consider picking sides.

The drama, which has played out for months in court and in dueling media appearances and leaks, has pitted Mr. Miller, 37 against his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, 32, who has accused him of abusing her and their toddler daughter. Mr. Miller has denied the claims and said that Ms. Moreno, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, also an Ohio Republican, is mentally unstable, accusing her of stalking and lying about him and endangering their daughter.

The concern from the highest levels of the Republican Party is not personal but political. The approaching ballot deadline has focused fresh attention on Mr. Miller’s case, including court filings that detail Ms. Moreno’s charges that he held a gun to her head, scalded her with water and fractured their daughter’s collarbone.

Mr. Moreno, who had initially made little in the way of public statements about the matter, issued a blistering one on Sunday calling his former son-in-law unfit for public office. But few other Republican leaders have openly criticized the congressman over the accusations, even as they privately worry that the scandal could put Ohio’s Seventh Congressional District at risk.

The district, which stretches from the Cleveland suburbs to Amish country, is solidly Republican. But with anti-Trump sentiment sweeping the country, it is not a lock, especially given that Mr. Miller’s Democratic challenger, Brian Poindexter, is a union ironworker who could appeal to working-class voters.

White House officials have been strategizing on how to most effectively prod Mr. Miller to withdraw. They have also explored possible replacements should Mr. Miller exit the race, according to a person familiar with the conversations.

Jane Timken, a state senator and former state party chair who unsuccessfully sought the G.O.P. nomination for Senate in 2022, has been floated as a possible alternate — though she has made clear that she does not want the job.

Mr. Miller, though, has insisted in private and public that he can still win a third term, and angrily rejected any suggestion that he step aside. He broadcast a lengthy livestream over the weekend in which he appeared agitated as he denied the allegations against him. On Tuesday, after having spoken with Mr. Trump, he announced that he would open an ethics investigation into himself “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family.”

Not long afterward, the House Ethics Committee said in a statement that it was “reviewing allegations that Representative Max Miller may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.”

A long paper trail of court filings, including for dueling restraining orders, as well as a file that Mr. Miller released on Sunday in an apparent effort to clear his name, paint the picture of an increasingly ugly family dispute in which each side has gone to great lengths to make the other look as violent, unstable and dishonest as possible.

The back-and-forth is full of tragic details, including a story that Mr. Moreno told on Tuesday at the Capitol, in which he said he had once picked up his granddaughter at a police station and that Mr. Miller had refused to hand over her favorite stuffed blue bunny.

Also on Tuesday, Ms. Moreno’s lawyers pointed to a picture of the couple’s toddler that had been included in the file Mr. Miller posted on Sunday and accused him of publishing an image that could be considered child sexual abuse material, noting that it had been viewed at least 204,000 times before it was removed.

A lawyer for Mr. Miller said the inclusion of the photograph was a mistake and that he had taken it down, according to Punchbowl News.

On the ground in Mr. Miller’s district this week, there was little sign of the chaos sweeping the race and alarming Republicans at the highest levels. Mr. Miller showed up on Monday at a county fair, where he campaigned before a hog show and among constituents who mostly said they had not heard about the week’s developments.

Local officials also stayed mostly silent about the race. Three of the four Republican county chairs in Mr. Miller’s district did not respond to questions on Monday about whether they supported his candidacy. Matt Miller, the chairman of Ashland County and the mayor of Ashland, said he “did not have a final opinion on the matter.”

Gov. Mike DeWine of Ohio, a Republican, told a reporter for Signal Ohio on Tuesday: “I’m not going to weigh in on it. These are very serious allegations that he vehemently denies.”

Vivek Ramaswamy, another Republican who is in a competitive race for governor, did not respond to inquiries about Max Miller’s situation. And Senator Jon Husted, who is facing his own tough race to keep his seat, told Newsmax on Tuesday only that he hoped “the president’s intervention can help move things along.”

Behind closed doors, however, some local officials were working to figure out how to compel Mr. Miller to step aside, according to two people briefed on the conversations, and what would happen if he did. They had come to the conclusion that only Mr. Trump himself had a chance of changing Mr. Miller’s mind.

Former Representative Jim Renacci, a Republican and former small-town mayor who represented a House district that covered much of the same area from 2011 to 2019, said he had been fielding calls about stepping in to seek the seat.

“I am convinced of this: The only person that would have a chance, and might not even have a chance, is me,” he said from a bench in downtown Wadsworth on Monday night, citing his name recognition in the district and the difficulties of running a potentially short race. “And even when I think of it, it would be a daunting challenge.”

Mr. Renacci also stopped short of saying that Mr. Miller should withdraw.

At the Medina County Fair, where Mr. Miller appeared on Monday, the Republican Party booth was advertising his picture next to a sign that said “RE-ELECT.”

Volunteers declined to discuss his campaign, saying only that they were praying for him.

Across the aisle, at the Democratic Party booth, volunteers were registering voters.

Tyler Pager contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Workers Disassemble Parts of Trump’s White House Helipad, Photos Show
item.description:
President Trump has been building a huge new helipad at the White House. But on Tuesday, workers seemed to be reversing course on the project.

As of last week, the helipad appeared to be nearing completion. After starting work in June, workers had built a circle 100 feet in diameter in the middle of the green expanse of the South Lawn. They were starting to add the finishing touches in granite, laying out the lettering of the presidential seal along the edge of the pad.

But then, on Sunday, photos showed that some of the lettering had been removed. Where it had said “Seal of the President of the United States,” only “eal of the” was left in place. By Tuesday, photos of the helipad showed all the granite letters were gone: It was back to what appeared to be bare concrete.

The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that Mr. Trump had ordered contractors to redo weeks of work on the project, unhappy that the helipad — like the South Lawn it sits on — had a noticeable slope.

A White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, declined on Tuesday to say why the helipad’s lettering had been removed, or what would be changed about the project.

Mr. Trump has said he needs a helipad on the South Lawn to accommodate a new kind of helicopter now used to transport him, under the call sign Marine One. The new helicopters, made by Sikorsky, produce engine exhaust so hot that it can scorch the grass.

“For years, the White House has desperately needed a proper Helipad on White House grounds that will allow the President to land safely and also protect the beautiful South Lawn grass from the fierce exhaust fumes of the incredible Marine One,” Mr. Ingle said in a statement.

Lockheed Martin, which owns Sikorsky, has said it is paying to build the helipad as a donation. Mr. Trump said it would cost between $5 million and $6 million.

The change would alter the character of the South Lawn, which has been used for social gatherings and White House events. Mr. Trump did not seek permission to build the helipad from Congress or from the architectural review panels that often vet projects in Washington’s monumental core. The White House has said that “operational upgrades” like this one do not need outside review.

item.title: Officials Say They’ve Found the Cause of a Fire That Devastated L.A.
item.description:
The deadly blaze that devastated the Altadena neighborhood in Los Angeles County early last year was ignited by a transmission tower belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday.

The county’s fire department said the blaze, which killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,400 buildings, was started by electrical sparks coming off the tower, according to a joint investigation by the department and Cal Fire, the state’s firefighting agency. The tower was out of service at the time.

Though Edison had previously acknowledged that its equipment most likely started the blaze, known as the Eaton fire, the cause had not been officially confirmed.

Fire officials took 18 months to review evidence with experts, including video footage that showed “an unknown burning material” falling from the tower to the dry vegetation below in the Eaton Canyon area, according to the report. The blaze ignited about 12 seconds later, officials said, quickly spreading into surrounding neighborhoods.

The Eaton fire, which ignited on Jan. 7, 2025, raged through Altadena during a catastrophic week in which another blaze killed 12 people in the Pacific Palisades, bringing the total death toll from the Los Angeles wildfires to 31.

Together, the blazes were the second deadliest wildfire disaster in state history, behind only the Camp fire, which tore through Paradise, Calif., in 2018, killing 85 people.

Federal prosecutors have accused a man who they say harbored resentments against the wealthy of setting the blaze in the Palisades, an affluent neighborhood stretching from the Pacific Ocean to the Santa Monica Mountains. A Los Angeles judge declared a mistrial last month after the jury failed to reach a verdict. The man, Jonathan Rinderknecht, will be retried in October.

Many months later, thousands of destroyed houses in both Altadena and the Pacific Palisades are being rebuilt or are in the planning stages. Thousands of other buildings remain damaged by smoke, leaving many residents with no clear path to safely return home. The fires are estimated to have caused up to $164 billion in total property and other losses.

Anthony C. Marrone, the county fire chief, said in a statement on Tuesday that he recognized that no investigation could ease the pain of residents affected by the Eaton fire.

“While the cause has been determined, our focus remains on assisting our residents to rebuild their homes and livelihoods, and ensuring lessons learned drive meaningful and impactful change in memory of the 19 lives lost,” Chief Marrone said.

On Tuesday, Kathleen Dunleavy, a spokeswoman for Southern California Edison, acknowledged the findings.

“We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the beginning,” she said. In a recent earnings call, company officials noted that their equipment was likely associated with the fire, she said, but they have also pointed out that wildfires of the Eaton fire’s magnitude “are rarely the result of a single factor.”

In October, the power company took the unusual step of establishing a compensation fund for victims even before fire investigators had determined the cause of the Eaton fire — a move that suggested that Edison had all but concluded that its lines had caused the blaze. It has committed hundred of millions of dollars in payments to victims.

The company has also filed lawsuits accusing government agencies and businesses of failing to warn residents of the fire and of not doing enough to prevent it from spreading.

For months, the utility and lawyers for customers had suspected that an inactive line might have been responsible for the Eaton fire. Even when out of service, the lines, sometimes referred to as “zombie” lines, can act as a conductor, picking up energy from active high-voltage lines nearby.

Investigators said that video footage obtained from a resident showed the moment the Eaton fire started, at about 6:11 p.m. on Jan. 7, 2025. The footage, they said, showed two bright blue and white flashes on the slope near the out-of-service tower, followed by an orange glow that appeared to be “dripping fire.” In interviews with investigators, several other residents described seeing flames under the tower.

Mikal Watts, a lawyer representing many Altadena residents who lost their homes, was among the people who had said earlier that an inactive power line may have been responsible for the fire.

“We are grateful that L.A. County took the time and the effort to review everything, and are pleased with its conclusions confirming our earlier work,” Mr. Watts said on Tuesday. “Edison must now pay for the $20 billion in damage it caused.”

item.title: Inside the Oval Office Showdown Between Trump and Jeanine Pirro
item.description:
Jeanine Pirro had had it up to here with Doug Burgum. The famously voluble U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia strode into the Oval Office late Monday with her future on the line and the interior secretary, whom she privately called an incompetent liar, in her cross hairs.

A few hours earlier — in front of the cameras, from the Resolute Desk — President Trump had accused Ms. Pirro, an ally and friend from New York going back decades, of “folding like an umbrella” and “choking” after she withdrew charges against a man accused of destroying the lining of his beloved but shoddily renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Why was he so angry at her? Because Ms. Pirro had dared to publicly demolish one of his most cherished narratives, promoted by Mr. Burgum, that vandals — and not a contractor hired by the Interior Department to do a rushed job — had defaced a Washington landmark.

Mr. Trump raged against Ms. Pirro in private on Monday. Then he raged a little to reporters. Rumors she would be fired burbled through West Wing. Then he raged a little bit more before hosting a high-drama, face-to-face meeting with Ms. Pirro at the White House worthy of two decorated veterans of confrontational reality TV.

Mr. Burgum had been invited too, so Ms. Pirro came prepared. She entered the White House from the West Executive driveway in a bright red blazer that matched her fight-back mood, schlepping a white box containing evidence, plus a black box with documents, on wheels.

Waiting for her in the Oval Office, along with the president: Mr. Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and David Warrington, the White House counsel.

After about an hour of intense back-and-forth, Ms. Pirro emerged with her job intact, for now.

During the meeting, Ms. Pirro, her voice raised at times, directly confronted Mr. Burgum, accusing him of misleading the president. She made the case that Mr. Burgum had promoted a self-serving cover story to conceal his own missteps.

Mr. Burgum spoke less, but did his best to defend himself, according to a person briefed on the exchange requesting anonymity to discuss internal conversations.

Mr. Trump seemed considerably less angry by day’s end, the person said.

Spokespeople for the White House, Ms. Pirro and Mr. Burgum did not respond to requests for comment.

This account, based on interviews with several people with knowledge of the events, demonstrated a core truth of Mr. Trump’s second term: Anyone willing to contradict the president is in trouble, even if the dissenter happens to be a family friend who has faithfully executed his prosecutorial agenda over the years.

The saga began on July 2, when a fired-up Ms. Pirro appeared before members of the news media to announce that her office had indicted David Hearn, 67, a former Olympic canoeist, on a single count of felony vandalism after he had been observed damaging the pool lining.

“This is not only a priority for the president, but for myself,” Ms. Pirro said, adding: “We will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Hearn willfully destroyed property.”

She did not. Last Friday, Ms. Pirro beat a humbling prosecutorial retreat in a 20-page court filing, admitting that her fast-track July indictment of the three-time Olympian had been based on false assumptions and incomplete evidence.

The document amounted to an indictment of sorts of Mr. Burgum; the contractor hired to repair the pool, Atlantic Industrial Coatings; and U.S. Park Police officials.

Ms. Pirro’s filing suggested that Mr. Burgum had committed the twofold sin of failing to competently oversee the renovation, then prodding Mr. Trump to accept the vandals-did-it story. Ms. Pirro said that her staff had relied almost exclusively on claims by Interior Department officials that extensive damage to the lining was caused by Mr. Hearn and other vandals who were observed tugging at or removing pieces of material from the wall.

After reviewing thousands of pages of evidence, she concluded the department had rushed and “botched” the renovation, and that bad information from Park Police officials had led her to cite “tremendous evidence” against Mr. Hearn that did not exist.

The whole episode had a vaguely comic air (why would the leader of the free world, juggling war and a wobbly economy, fixate on a pool liner?). But consequences for Mr. Hearn were anything but. The felony charge carried a maximum 10-year prison term, based on an assessment by Ms. Pirro’s team that the damage inflicted amounted to more than $1,000.

Ms. Pirro knew full well that her U-turn could infuriate Mr. Trump, but decided to cram her filing with enough evidence to decisively disprove Mr. Burgum’s claims.

She gave the White House a heads-up last week before filing the motion to dismiss the charge against Mr. Hearn in federal court, although it was not clear if Mr. Trump was briefed, according to people familiar with the situation who requested anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

Ominous signals from Mr. Trump began to emerge on Saturday morning, a day after Ms. Pirro filed her motion.

“I disagree 100 percent with Jeanine Pirro,” Mr. Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM.” He added, “There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!”

Mr. Burgum took to social media to defend himself soon afterward. His staff “provided the U.S. attorney’s office expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool,” he wrote.

Mr. Trump seems at first to have taken Mr. Burgum’s side, and grew steadily angrier at Ms. Pirro as the weekend ground on.

By mid-Monday, he pounced when asked a Pirro question at a press availability in the Oval Office, saying he was disappointed and accusing Ms. Pirro of being too afraid to present the case to the judge in the Hearn case.

Notably, he did not answer a question from a reporter about Ms. Pirro’s future employment.

Why Ms. Pirro, who knows Mr. Trump’s personality and trigger points better than almost anyone outside his family, was willing to risk the president’s wrath remains somewhat unclear.

After reviewing thousands of pages of evidence over the past few weeks, Ms. Pirro determined the Hearn indictment needed to be rescinded before it was thrown out of court, according to two people close to the situation.

Her critics have questioned whether her motive was nearly so straightforward or altruistic.

They suggest that Ms. Pirro’s decision to withdraw the indictment was self-protective: She might be trying to head off disciplinary action that could result if grand jury testimony or other internal materials are made public. Mr. Hearn’s lawyers said she was guilty of what she had accused Mr. Burgum of doing — rushing to take an action to appease her boss — and that she had ample access, before indicting Mr. Hearn, to evidence showing that the damage had been caused by the contractor.

The contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, has not responded to queries about the case, but a June 21 statement on the company’s website says there are “some areas” of the pool that require repairs.

Ms. Pirro, who rose to prominence in the jostling New York City tabloid market alongside Mr. Trump, has also demonstrated a greater sense of independence than many other senior department officials, whose careers have been entirely made (and can be unmade) by Mr. Trump.

She left a far higher-paying job at Fox News to take over the U.S. attorney job, is lukewarm on Washington, and has told friends (some of them skeptical) that she sees her current post as a capstone, not a steppingstone, and does not fear a “you’re fired” moment.

Yet, by all accounts, Ms. Pirro offered a spirited defense of herself on Monday, and appears determined to win her battle with Mr. Burgum and, eventually, win back Mr. Trump.

David A. Fahrenthold and Maxine Joselow contributed reporting.

item.title: Missouri Says Voters Cannot Decide on Redrawn Congressional Districts
item.description:
Missouri voters cannot weigh in on whether to keep congressional district boundaries that were redrawn to benefit Republicans, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said on Tuesday, even though opponents of the new map had gathered thousands of signatures seeking a statewide vote.

The decision, which was announced on Election Day while primary voters were at the polls, was widely expected to be challenged in court. Opponents of the redrawn map have signaled that they will ask judges to place the referendum on the November ballot and to revert to the old congressional map for the general election.

“Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” said Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that proposed the referendum. “We’ve fought back against politicians for the last year,” he added in a statement, “and we won’t stop now.”

The status of Missouri’s congressional districts has been unclear for months, even as candidates were campaigning and voters casting primary ballots in the newly redrawn districts.

Mr. Hoskins, a Republican, waited months to make a decision on whether the proposed referendum qualified for the ballot, drawing complaints from opponents of redistricting. Those people and groups insisted that they had submitted more than enough signatures and that the old district lines should apply until a referendum is held.

Mr. Hoskins said he believed that Missouri law did not allow for a congressional map to be challenged in a referendum and that he was prepared to defend that decision in court.

He declined to say how many valid signatures had been submitted and whether that number would have been sufficient to place the question on the ballot had he found the referendum to be constitutional.

“At issue is not the number of signatures turned in,” he told reporters, “but the fact that the referendum itself is null and void by virtue of the fact that it is unconstitutional.”

Missouri law allows residents to gather signatures to challenge legislation. If enough signatures are gathered, the legislation is paused until a statewide vote is held. By waiting to make a decision on the petitions until the deadline on Tuesday, Mr. Hoskins might have increased the odds that the new map is used in November, even if the courts eventually decide that voters should weigh in on the referendum.

Residents started collecting signatures last year shortly after Republican lawmakers passed the new congressional map, which was designed to flip one of the state’s two Democratic-held U.S. House seats. Missouri was among the first states to join President Trump’s national push to redraw district boundaries to improve Republicans’ odds of keeping House control in the midterms. Some Democratic-led states responded by proposing new boundaries of their own.

The Missouri Supreme Court ruled that lawmakers had acted within their authority when they redrew the map outside the usual once-a-decade cycle.

The map passed by Republicans last year sliced the core of Kansas City, Mo., into three districts and left Representative Emanuel Cleaver, a long-serving Democrat who was also Kansas City’s first Black mayor, with a Republican-leaning district that includes faraway rural counties. The new map did not significantly change the makeup of Missouri’s other Democratic-held district, in the St. Louis area.

The fate of Missouri’s map could help determine partisan control of the House during the final two years of Mr. Trump’s term.

After a brief pause, redistricting efforts ramped up again this spring after the Supreme Court raised the bar for bringing challenges under the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Several Republican-led Southern states redrew their maps after the ruling, positioning the party to pick up several seats in the midterms.

item.title: Maryland Lawmakers Back Amendment Giving Democrats 2028 Advantage
item.description:
Maryland lawmakers passed a constitutional amendment on Tuesday that would make it easier for the legislature to redraw the state’s congressional map and shift the one Republican-held House seat to Democrats in the 2028 elections.

Democrats hold seven of the state’s eight congressional seats, and they tried to join a redistricting wave over the last year as the two parties jockeyed for control of the House in the next Congress.

But a gerrymandered map that was approved by the Maryland House of Delegates in February and would have all but locked up that eighth congressional seat couldn’t clear the Democratic-controlled State Senate. Bill Ferguson, the senate president, had resisted the redistricting push, arguing that drawing a new map was too risky, given that a state judge ruled in 2022 that an attempt had violated the Maryland Constitution.

If Maryland had adopted this year’s map, the state would have joined California, Missouri and other states in crafting new districts for the 2026 midterms. This unusual burst of redistricting, which usually occurs early each decade after the results of the U.S. census, was set in motion by President Trump in early 2025, when he urged Texas politicians to redraw the state’s congressional map in a bid to ensure his party retained control of the U.S. House. Republicans currently hold a slim majority.

But despite intense pressure from some Maryland Democratic leaders, the regular legislative session ended in April without the House’s new map coming up for a vote in the State Senate.

Then, after the Supreme Court’s decision in May gutting the Voting Rights Act, Mr. Ferguson said the state “must respond as the ground shifts under us.” Two months later, state Democratic leaders announced that the legislature would reconvene for a special session to consider an amendment putting lawmakers on stronger legal footing for redistricting.

The special session began on Monday and the amendment that passed on Tuesday will go before voters in November. It would establish that congressional districts are not subject to the same constitutional requirements as state legislative districts, namely that they be compact, and that they consider natural boundaries and city and county lines. The judge who struck down the redistricting attempt in 2022 had cited those requirements in her decision.

While some Democrats grumbled that the monthslong dispute about process kept Maryland from adopting a new map in time for this year’s midterms, the amendment would clear the way for new districts heading into 2028. Multiple states, including New York and Mississippi, have already started exploring the process of redistricting for the next cycle.

Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, praised the passage of the amendment.

“Maryland will not be caught flat-footed while Republicans engage in political redlining that guts decades of progress that the generations before us fought for,” he said in a statement after the vote.

The leader of the Republican minority in the House, Jason Buckel, decried the amendment. “When history judges the actions of the General Assembly in years to come, what has happened in Annapolis this week will be seen as a sad chapter in the institution’s history,” he said in a statement.
