item.title: Judge Pained as He Grants Dismissal of Jan. 6 Charges Against Oath Keepers
item.description:
A federal judge expressed deep regret on Tuesday as he granted a request by the Justice Department to throw out criminal charges against eight members of the far-right Oath Keepers militia who were charged with seditious conspiracy for the central role they played in the storming of the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

The move by the judge, Amit P. Mehta, came less than a month after one of his colleagues in Federal District Court in Washington made a similarly pained decision to dismiss Jan. 6-related charges against five members of another far-right group, the Proud Boys, who also played a key part in the Capitol attack. The twin rulings, which both judges made claiming that their hands were tied by the law, amounted to a final erasure of the vast investigation into Jan. 6, the largest criminal inquiry undertaken in the Justice Department’s 156-year history.

Confessing that he wished for “a different ending,” Judge Mehta blasted the Justice Department’s request for a dismissal in the case, saying it bestowed “unearned grace” on the Oath Keepers defendants — including on their leader Stewart Rhodes — “by wiping their records clean.”

He also took pains to recall the profound damage that occurred on Jan. 6 to people at the Capitol as well as to the nation’s politics, refusing to ignore either one as President Trump has sought to play down the violence of the attack and has repeatedly asserted that the rioters themselves were wronged by efforts to hold them accountable and deserve financial restitution.

“Today’s epilogue diminishes the gravity of that day,” Judge Mehta wrote, “denigrates the work of the prosecutors and law enforcement officers who secured these convictions, and excuses criminal acts that caused a centuries-long pillar of our democracy — the peaceful transfer of presidential power — to buckle.”

In an almost elegiac tone, Judge Mehta, an Obama appointee, acknowledged that he was bound to “give way to the primacy of the executive branch,” which has wide latitude in making decisions in criminal prosecutions. But the judge seemed unable to bite his tongue entirely, chiding the prosecutors who had requested the dismissal even as he acceded to them.

“If it is their view that the public interest is served by surrendering convictions for crimes against the country to the gloss of an enduring public record, then that is an assessment to which this court must yield,” he wrote.

Prosecutors first requested that the charges be dropped in May. They noted that Mr. Rhodes and his co-defendants had not been fully pardoned, but had only had their sentences commuted, when Mr. Trump issued a sweeping grant of clemency to all of the Jan. 6 rioters on his first day back in the White House.

In their request to dismiss the charges outright, prosecutors had claimed that it was in the “interest of justice” — a notion that Judge Mehta scoffed at in his ruling. He pointed out that the government had never said that the charges against the Oath Keepers were “legally deficient” or that the evidence presented at two separate trials was insufficient to sustain their convictions.

Moreover, the Justice Department, he went on, never admitted to prosecutorial misconduct or identified any legal error that could have resulted in an unfair trial or a wrongful conviction. This was a not-so-subtle rebuttal of arguments that Mr. Trump and his allies have often made.

Judge Mehta spent the first three pages of his ruling reciting what Mr. Rhodes and his co-defendants did on Jan. 6. He recalled how some members of the Oath Keepers were stationed in Virginia as a “quick reaction force” to support their compatriots at the Capitol and had assembled an arsenal of weapons that one witness at the trial described as the largest cache of firearms he had seen since serving in the military.

In the run-up to Jan. 6, several of the defendants made remarks on group chats embracing violence, Judge Mehta noted.

One of them, David Moerschel, wrote on Christmas Day in 2020: “It’s a war time Christmas. Gentleman, Trump is going to make his big move on Jan 6. Be prepared.”

On New Year’s Eve, Mr. Rhodes wrote in another group chat: “On the 6th, they are going to put the final nail in the coffin of this Republic, unless we fight our way out. With Trump (preferably) or without him, we have no choice.”

On Jan. 6 itself, nearly a dozen Oath Keepers, wearing military gear, marched up the eastern steps of the Capitol and entered the building. Half of them headed toward the Senate chamber, Judge Mehta wrote, where they sought to storm past a line of police officers. The others ended up in front of Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office.

Later, one of the Oath Keepers, Kelly Meggs, boasted to a friend, “We looked for her.”

item.title: When to Expect Results in Michigan, Virginia, Missouri, Washington and Kansas
item.description:
Five states are holding primaries on Tuesday. Here’s when to expect results.

Voting in Michigan is decentralized, meaning each county presides over its own system.

The polls close for most of the state at 8 p.m. Eastern time. Major cities like Detroit, which is part of Wayne County, may still be receiving large numbers of absentee ballots at that hour. Officials say most counties could have their unofficial results in by midnight on Tuesday, but late ballot deliveries in larger jurisdictions could delay the results until early Wednesday morning. They caution that it could take as long as 24 hours before all results are in.

Most of Michigan is in the Eastern time zone, but four counties are on Central time and their polling locations will close an hour later than the rest of the state’s. After polls close across the state and each county uploads its results, you can check the numbers on The Times’s results tracker.

These results will remain unofficial until Aug. 24, the deadline for Michigan’s Board of State Canvassers to certify the vote.

The top county and local election officials in Virginia, called general registrars, will enter results as they come in after polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern. Election officials anticipate that most results will be in by late Tuesday or early Wednesday morning.

Follow along with the Virginia results as they are reported live on Tuesday.

All results are unofficial until the election is certified by the State Board of Elections on Aug. 18.

Once polls close at 7 p.m. local time (8 p.m. Eastern), Missouri’s jurisdictions will begin sending in results. Officials anticipate that results will come more slowly from the larger precincts — such as those in Missouri’s most populous county, St. Louis — and those with more cumbersome equipment.

Officials expect at least a partial report from most jurisdictions by around 10 or 11 p.m. local time (11 p.m. or midnight Eastern).

The Times has a tracker for Missouri’s votes as they come in; follow along here. Official results won’t come until the morning of Aug. 25, when the state’s board of canvassers is set to meet to certify the results.

Results will start coming in after polls close at 7 p.m. local time (8 p.m. Eastern). Election officials noted two factors that might delay results. First, each county chooses its own ballot tabulation methods, meaning some results might come later than others. Second, four Kansas counties are in the Mountain Daylight time zone rather than Central, so polling places there will close an hour later than the rest of the state.

Officials predict all counties will have their results up on their websites by the end of the night. Follow along with the results as they come in with The Times’s tracker.

The state Board of Canvassers will convene by Sept. 1 to certify the vote.

Washington is one of several states that send mail ballots to all registered voters, and election officials expect the first round of results soon after 8 p.m. local time (11 p.m. Eastern).

The state is holding top two primaries for various races, which means that all candidates are listed on the same ballot, regardless of party, and the top two vote-getters will advance to the general election.

In a typical election, most or all counties report initial unofficial results around 8:30 p.m. local time (11:30 p.m. Eastern), though this depends on how many ballots are turned in early. In close races, election officials warn, it can take several days to know the final result.

You can visit The Times’s vote tracker here.

On Aug. 21, the secretary of state’s office will certify the consolidated statewide totals and the primary results will be official.

item.title: Spending Tied to AIPAC Dominated the Michigan Senate Primary
item.description:
Rarely is the top issue in a high-profile election how, exactly, the contest has been funded.

But that has been the case in the Democratic primary race for Senate in Michigan, which has inflamed so many of the party’s explosive political debates.

Representative Haley Stevens, the moderate establishment-backed candidate, benefited from about $62 million in advertising spending from half a dozen outside groups. Over half of that sum came from the super PAC arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the country’s most influential pro-Israel group.

That spending gave her and her allies about a 9-to-1 spending advantage over her progressive rival, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, and his allies, according to data from the media tracking firm AdImpact. Two main ads from the group targeted Dr. El-Sayed over his past criticisms of women like Michelle Obama and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan and featured positive comments about Ms. Stevens from former President Barack Obama as part of her attempt to appeal to Black voters.

But Dr. El-Sayed spun the barrage of spending into an attack line, turning Ms. Stevens’s support from AIPAC in particular into a political liability in a state with a heavy Muslim population. He argued that Ms. Stevens would seek only incremental change because she was close to corporate donors.

Last week, at the final debate, the two candidates spent much of the first 15 minutes in a searing fight about super PACs, advertising trends and dark-money nonprofit groups with undisclosed donors. The clash underscored the central role that money in politics came to play in the contest.

In response to the very first question of the debate, Dr. El-Sayed called out Ms. Stevens for a pro-Israel vote she had recently cast. “That is the pro quo that comes with the quid,” he said, adding, “It really comes down to how you are funded.”

Ms. Stevens has not engaged much with questions about AIPAC support. In an interview published last week, she said some voters had “campaign finance zoomies” and stressed that other issues were much more important.

In his own much more limited advertising, including a closing spot featuring Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Dr. El-Sayed has called for less money in politics.

In recent years, the Democratic Party has been entangled in emotional debates about the United States’ relationship to Israel. Those arguments have often included a focus on the role of big-spending outside groups in elections, as left-wing activists seek to make AIPAC and its affiliated groups toxic and to politically punish Democrats who take their money.

And there has been a lot of that money in Michigan. The $31.9 million poured into ads in the state by AIPAC’s main super PAC, the United Democracy Project, is the most spent by a single group in a federal Democratic primary this cycle, according to AdImpact data. That makes Tuesday a test for AIPAC unlike any other that the big-money group has faced this cycle.

Dr. El-Sayed has also sought to highlight just how much of the pro-Stevens spending is being financed by donors whose identities remain hidden.

The United Democracy Project’s biggest donor is AIPAC, a nonprofit that does not disclose its donors. And all of the other pro-Stevens groups are financed by nonprofit groups that do not disclose their donors; are dark-money nonprofits themselves; or began spending late enough in the election cycle that they have yet to file paperwork with the Federal Election Commission that could reveal their donors.

Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

item.title: What Was on the Minds of Michigan Voters? Many Cited the Economy and Trump.
item.description:
The hard-fought Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, which pits Dr. Abdul El-Sayed against Representative Haley Stevens, has often been described as a battle over whether the Democratic Party should move to the left or the center as well as a referendum on Israel.

But what was on the minds of voters on Tuesday as they cast their ballots?

Pre-primary polling on which issues have been motivating voters, while limited, pointed to a Democratic primary electorate that was deeply concerned about the economy and President Trump. Issues related to Israel, Gaza or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which opposes Dr. El-Sayed and has spent heavily on the race supporting Ms. Stevens, were not cited among top concerns.

Nineteen percent of likely Democratic primary voters listed opposition to Mr. Trump and Republicans as the main motivation for their vote in a recent Detroit News/ WDIV-TV poll. Effectively tied for first place, at 18 percent, were concerns about the economy and the cost of living. A small but sizable share — 12 percent — said they were focused on electing Democrats and taking back control of the U.S. Senate.

Here are the issues that some voters said they were motivated by:

Sarah Swider, 54, a professor at Wayne State University, said she was concerned that too many people lacked access to health care and that she was voting for Dr. El-Sayed. “We are one of the richest nations in the world, if not the richest,” she said. Ms. Swider added that in other countries she has lived in, “they all have health care for all.”

Delilah Reynolds Fields, a 56-year-old bakery owner in Detroit, said the price of gas and other rising costs of living were having a “very direct” effect on her business and were the biggest factor in her voting decisions.

“I feel the impact,” she said, adding, “I think it’s affecting everyone.”

She has voted for Democrats and Republicans, she added, saying that she feels “politically homeless” and that the Democratic Party takes voters like her for granted. But she voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, she said. This year, she has a “pretty strong sense” that she will vote for Democrats in November. She declined to say whom she voted for Tuesday.

Regina Mines, 61, of Detroit said her biggest concern was a sense that Mr. Trump was “humiliating” the United States internationally and dividing the country domestically. His second term has, in her view, been far worse than his first, she added, citing his politicization of the Justice Department and the war with Iran, among other issues.

“We look really bad around the world, and the office is not being upheld like it should be,” said Ms. Mines, a retiree who had worked in health insurance. “I’m embarrassed about his language. The way he carries himself. The way he talks about people. It’s just embarrassing.”

Ms. Mines said she voted for Ms. Stevens for Senate because of how she had helped the auto industry under the administration of Barack Obama, her favorite president.

Jack Gruszczynski, 34, a museum educator at the Detroit Institute of Arts, said he was focused on one issue: limiting data centers in Michigan.

“I really feel like Gretchen Whitmer, who’s a governor who I’ve loved for most of her time here, has really failed Michiganders in the last few months of her time by allowing data centers to come into the state,” said Mr. Gruszczynski. (Ms. Whitmer pushed for a law that offered tax incentives for data centers.) He said he was voting for Dr. El-Sayed on Tuesday, but that in November he could be open to supporting a Republican for the first time if one had a strong stance against data centers.

While Israel and Gaza did not necessarily show up as particularly motivating to voters in polling results, that may be a reflection of the polling landscape in this primary. Most polls did not even ask voters about their top issues, and the ones that did so asked in a limited fashion.

AIPAC spent more than $30 million on ads and outreach to promote Ms. Stevens, who has been supportive of Israel, over Dr. El-Sayed, who has said he believes that Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza.

But for many Democratic primary voters in Michigan, affiliation with AIPAC can be a liability. A majority of the state’s likely Democratic primary voters viewed the organization negatively in a poll conducted by Data for Progress, a Democratic polling firm. However, 40 percent of voters had not heard of the organization.

Mira Hughes, 22, of Hamtramck, said she was supporting Dr. El-Sayed because “he’s going to get into office and make sure that our tax dollars don’t go to Israel to bomb children.”

Nada Chamoun, 49, a real estate agent in Dearborn, Mich., said after voting, “I don’t want this war.”

Ms. Chamoun, who voted for Dr. El-Sayed, said she typically split her ballot in general elections, voting based on individual candidates. But this November, she said, she planned to vote only for Democrats because of the “state of the world we’re in right now.” She is concerned about how the conflict is affecting the cost of living, she said.

item.title: Polls Show El-Sayed With a Significant Edge in Michigan Senate Primary
item.description:
Recent polls of Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary have shown a comfortable lead for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, over Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate four-term congresswoman. However, some uncertainty remains, given how difficult it is to predict who will turn out for primaries, an issue that has sometimes led to surprising outcomes.

The race for the Democratic nomination sharpened in early July when Mallory McMorrow, a state senator, dropped out (her name will still appear on the ballot). Since Ms. McMorrow’s exit, Dr. El-Sayed has clear leads of more than 10 percentage points in seven of the nine polls fielded.

Ms. Stevens’s only leads in that stretch came from a Glengariff Group survey fielded shortly after Ms. McMorrow’s exit — where Ms. Stevens led by seven percentage points — and a Tavern Research poll from that same week. The Tavern poll showed her ahead by one percentage point head-to-head, but also had Dr. El-Sayed ahead by three percentage points when Ms. McMorrow was included in the question.

Polls from “select pollsters” meet certain criteria for reliability and are shown with a diamond.

Polls collected by The New York Times

Even when Ms. McMorrow was still in the race, Dr. El-Sayed led in most polls, though his leads at that point were mostly in the single digits. As the field has narrowed and undecided voters have broken, his margins have grown.

Polls collected by The New York Times. Previous results range from mid-April to early July. Margins are calculated as the difference between El-Sayed's and Stevens' vote shares, regardless of how McMorrow performed.

Poll results among demographic subgroups should be interpreted with caution, as they are based on relatively small subsamples that are not necessarily designed to be representative. But some meaningful takeaways can emerge when multiple surveys point in the same direction. Polls in this race have consistently showed Dr. El-Sayed performing well among voters under 30 years old — a persistent trend among recent progressive candidates — and have him maintaining an overall advantage with voters under 50 years old.

Ms. Stevens, by contrast, draws her strongest support from older voters. That could play a key role in how the race plays out, as that demographic has historically made up a significant share of primary electorates.

Some concerns have been voiced that Dr. El-Sayed’s progressive views could make him a riskier general-election candidate. A recent SoCal Strategies poll — sponsored by Red Eagle Politics, a conservative personality — offered some support for that concern. In that poll, only 57 percent of Ms. Stevens’s primary supporters said they would back Dr. El-Sayed in the general if he won the nomination, and 12 percent said they would instead vote for former Representative Mike Rogers, the presumptive Republican nominee, who lost to Senator Elissa Slotkin in the 2024 general election.

Polls from “select pollsters” meet certain criteria for reliability and are shown with a diamond.

Polls collected by The New York Times

An EPIC-MRA poll showed Ms. Stevens leading Mr. Rogers by two percentage points, while Dr. El-Sayed lagged behind Mr. Rogers by three percentage points. A Glengariff Group poll from late July told a similar story, with Ms. Stevens in the lead by one percentage point (Dr. El-Sayed again trailed, this time by 10 percentage points).

On the opposite side of the Democratic spectrum, concerns have been raised that Ms. Stevens’s support for Israel could alienate other portions of the Democratic base. A late June Quantus survey found both Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed leading Mr. Rogers by one percentage point, while a Wedgewood poll from around the same time showed Dr. El-Sayed ahead of Mr. Rogers by five percentage points, and Ms. Stevens tied. More recently, a Mitchell poll conducted in late July found Dr. El-Sayed tied with Mr. Rogers, while Ms. Stevens lagged by three percentage points.

item.title: Luria Wins House Primary in Virginia, Setting Up a Rematch With Kiggans
item.description:
Former Representative Elaine Luria won the Democratic nomination for the Second Congressional District of Virginia on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, setting up a high-stakes general election rematch against Representative Jen Kiggans, a Republican, in one of the most competitive House districts in the nation.

Ms. Luria, who served in the U.S. Navy, was part of a class of moderate military veterans who helped Democrats flip the House in 2018. In Congress, she took on a prominent and politically risky role serving on the House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, saying at the time that “If I don’t get re-elected because of this, that’s OK.”

She did lose in 2022 as redistricting helped Ms. Kiggans, also a Navy veteran and a former helicopter pilot, defeat Ms. Luria in the Virginia Beach-area district.

The district, which is home to one of the highest concentrations of military veterans in the country, is the most competitive in Virginia. It tends to flip back and forth between the parties, and it is widely regarded as a genuine swing district again this year.

In one potentially encouraging sign for Democrats, Abigail Spanberger — a Democrat who served with Ms. Luria after also being elected to the House in 2018 — performed strongly in the area during her successful race for governor last year.

President Trump has never won a general election in Virginia, a state with tens of thousands of federal employees that was hit hard by his administration’s cuts to the federal work force, though he appeared to have won the Second District by less than one percentage point in 2024, according to data from the Virginia Public Access Project.

As Mr. Trump’s approval rating continues to sink nationally, Ms. Luria has sought to tie Ms. Kiggans to his administration at every turn.

Ms. Kiggans promised when she was sworn in that she would demonstrate “independent leadership” in Congress — a pledge, Democrats argue, she has not upheld.

item.title: Democrat Quits Senate Race in South Dakota, Clearing Way for Independent
item.description:
There is no primary in South Dakota on Tuesday, but there was a major development in that state’s Senate race: Julian Beaudion, the Democratic nominee, dropped out, clearing the way for an independent candidate to challenge Senator Mike Rounds, the Republican incumbent.

“While this decision is heartbreaking, it is not defeat,” Mr. Beaudion said in a statement.

The deadline to withdraw from the ballot was Tuesday. As recently as Monday, Mr. Beaudion had told The Washington Post that efforts to get him to drop out amounted to “political extortion.”

Mr. Beaudion said in the statement that the factors in his withdrawal included a “devastating house fire,” as well as “intimidating threats to drop out of this race.”

“The mental and physical safety of my family is my priority and for this reason alone, I step aside,” he said.

Brian Bengs, the independent candidate, previously ran for Senate as a Democrat in 2022, when he lost in a landslide to Senator John Thune, a Republican who is now the majority leader. In a social media post on Tuesday night, Mr. Bengs said that Mr. Beaudion had made a “patriotic decision to make this a two-person race.”

Mr. Beaudion said in the statement that he would “not be endorsing or supporting Brian Bengs in this race.”

Mr. Beaudion’s withdrawal from the race is the third this year by a Democratic Senate nominee in a red state, and in each case the withdrawal cleared the way for an independent candidate. The other states were Nebraska and Idaho.

Some Democrats have also pushed for Alani Bankhead, the party’s nominee in Montana, to quit the race and clear the path for Seth Bodnar, an independent in that state.

item.title: Shannon Taylor Wins Democratic Primary for Virginia House Race
item.description:
See the latest results in today’s key races including updates on the Michigan Senate primary, plus more elections in Michigan, Missouri, Kansas, Virginia and Washington.

Shannon Taylor, a prosecutor who pitched herself as a law-and-order Democrat, clinched the Democratic nomination in the seven-way primary for Virginia’s First Congressional District on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

The win sets her up to challenge Representative Rob Wittman, a Republican who was first elected two decades ago, for a seat that Democrats see as one of their best opportunities for a flip in November.

Fresh off a narrow loss in the Democratic primary for Virginia attorney general last fall, Ms. Taylor enjoyed strong backing from the party establishment. She drew on her record as the district attorney in Henrico County, in the Richmond suburbs, including a 90 percent conviction rate in local homicide cases during her nearly 15 years in office, on the campaign trail.

Her candidacy in a bellwether district could help Democrats test the appeal of more moderate candidates. Democrats also hope Ms. Taylor can thwart Republicans’ arguments that the party is soft on crime.

Ms. Taylor has already previewed the case she’ll make against Mr. Wittman, portraying him as a Washington insider who has profited from stock trading and tax breaks that he voted for. On Tuesday night, she promised she would represent a broad coalition of voters — not just Democrats — in the House.

“This campaign is for everyone,” Ms. Taylor wrote in a post on X. “Democrats, Republicans, and Independents who are tired of career politicians like Rob Wittman putting Washington insiders ahead of the people they represent."

A spokesman for Mr. Wittman’s campaign criticized Ms. Taylor for supporting an end to cash bail and for pushing to repeal mandatory minimum prison sentences.

“Congressman Wittman has a proven record of delivering for Virginia’s First District by lowering costs for families, strengthening our military, supporting law enforcement and working to keep Virginia communities safe,” Will Dieterich, Mr. Wittman’s campaign manager, said in a news release on Tuesday night. He added: “Virginians deserve a representative who will put public safety first — not experiment with it.”

The House Democratic campaign arm endorsed Ms. Taylor and pledged to spend on her behalf in the general election. Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat who previously represented a large portion of the district in Congress, also backed Ms. Taylor in the primary.

The establishment’s early support raised tensions between Ms. Taylor and her opponents, four of whom jointly wrote a letter asking the Democratic Party of Virginia to reaffirm neutrality in the race.

The district stretches from the Richmond suburbs to the so-called Historic Triangle of Jamestown, Yorktown, and Williamsburg, and out to the Tidewater region on the state’s eastern shore. While President Trump won the district by five points in 2024, the district has been trending to the left. Ms. Spanberger narrowly won the district in November, giving the party hope that it can continue the momentum and flip the seat.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the district as slightly right-leaning in November, while Fox News classified it in July as one of 16 tossup House districts.

Democrats had hoped that Ms. Taylor would face an easier general election race: Mr. Wittman would have had almost no path to victory under a voter-approved plan to gerrymander Virginia’s congressional district lines in Democrats’ favor. But the state Supreme Court blocked that map in May, locking in place the district lines for the 2026 midterm cycle.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official running on a progressive, anti-establishment platform, is one of two contenders in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Dr. El-Sayed, 41, of Ann Arbor, Mich., who, if elected in November, would become the first Muslim senator. He is running to replace Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat who is retiring.

1. He is supported by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Dr. El-Sayed has generated a deep well of left-wing support. He supports universal health care, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending U.S. aid to Israel. He is a vocal critic of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. He is backed by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and other left-wing leaders. But Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who is selective about intervening in Democratic primaries, is perhaps Dr. El-Sayed’s most important backer. Citing his communication skills, she says Dr. El-Sayed is more electable than his rival, Representative Haley Stevens. The Democratic establishment argues she is a better general election candidate, pointing to her centrist positions. He has separated himself from some of his progressive supporters by saying he is a capitalist, not a socialist.

2. He’s known for his rhetorical skill and his sharp personal attacks. Dr. El-Sayed, a former podcaster and CNN commentator, is a smooth communicator. Ms. Stevens has acknowledged he is a “talented guy” but has cast him as a “celebrity candidate.” In an interview, Dr. El-Sayed described the attack line as “odd,” and recalled his work in “the bowels of city government and Wayne County government.” Dr. El-Sayed also throws rhetorical punches. He has suggested Ms. Stevens has neither a “personality” nor a “message,” and he has dismissed her as the “least capable candidate in America.”

3. He ran for governor in 2018. Dr. El-Sayed tried to use a similar message that year, and he was also backed by Ms. Ocasio-Cortez. But he was handily defeated by Gretchen Whitmer, a moderate Democrat who went on to win the general election. Ms. Whitmer, now in her second term as governor, has endorsed Ms. Stevens. In an interview, Dr. El-Sayed said his message in 2018 was “a little bit premature for most folks.” That message, he added, was that Donald J. Trump’s victory in 2016 was not a “cosmic mistake” but a natural backlash to a political system “rigged” against Americans. But now, Dr. El-Sayed argued, Democratic voters are “looking for fighters who are going to stand up not just to the worst symptom of the disease”

4. He drew scrutiny by campaigning with a provocative streamer. Dr. El-Sayed has been joined on the trail by the popular streamer Hasan Piker, a critic of the Israeli government who has made incendiary comments. Jewish organizations and some Democrats have accused Mr. Piker of antisemitism (he rejects the claim), and some Democrats assailed Dr. El-Sayed for campaigning with him. Dr. El-Sayed responded by saying that Mr. Piker “speaks to an audience that too few Democrats are listening to or speaking to” and that Democrats “should have learned more lessons from the cancel culture wars.”

5. He is the son of Egyptian immigrants. Dr. El-Sayed was born in Michigan, and his first language was Arabic. As a youth, he struggled to fit in. After the Sept. 11 attacks, he was called anti-Arab slurs. On the campaign trail, he speaks of America’s promise and flaws. “I know what America can do for somebody,” he said at one rally. “I just know that too often America does not do that for too many of her kids.”

item.title: Chipotle Removes Jalapeños Linked to Salmonella Outbreak From Its Restaurants
item.description:
A salmonella outbreak that has sickened dozens of people in Minnesota prompted Chipotle Mexican Grill to announce on Tuesday that it was pulling certain jalapeños from its restaurants.

In a statement, the company said “Chipotle has removed the suspect jalapeños across all of our restaurants where they had been distributed and replaced them with jalapeños from different growers.” It was unclear how many restaurants were affected and in which states.

Laurie Schalow, the chief corporate affairs and food safety officer for Chipotle, highlighted the company’s “robust ingredient traceability system,” and said in the statement that it had “proactively identified jalapeños as a potential common ingredient from a common lot.”

The Minnesota Department of Health said it had identified 110 salmonella cases in this outbreak — and 75 of those people had reported having eaten at Chipotle between June 14 and July 14.

Other cases reported in Minnesota pointed to possible salmonella from other Mexican-style restaurants. The Food and Drug Administration lists “Salmonella Javiana” as an active investigation, with a possible 200-plus cases. The F.D.A. has not issued a recall or released findings but said online that it had initiated sampling.

“It is too soon for us to know if the outbreak is ongoing,” Carlota Medus, a top official in the foodborne diseases unit in Minnesota’s health department, said in a statement. “Given the measures Chipotle put in place, we are not concerned about Chipotle; but it is possible that the outbreak is ongoing if the contaminated food item is being served elsewhere. We do expect the case count to increase even if the illnesses occurred a couple of weeks ago, since it takes us a while to detect cases in surveillance.”

Chipotle has worked for years to improve its reputation after coming under immense scrutiny during a 2015 e. coli outbreak, which dealt the company a significant financial blow. In 2016, Chipotle started new marketing campaigns aimed at winning back customers.

Chipotle restaurants in Minnesota were specifically affected by the e. coli outbreak. That time, tomatoes were identified as the culprit.

The salmonella outbreak is the latest this summer in the United States, and the latest to involve Mexican-style food. Taco Bell became the early face of a cyclospora outbreak, but its sales have been recovering. Its parent company, Yum Brands, said transparency around pulling affected lettuce from stores had helped Taco Bell regain consumer trust.

item.title: Counties to Watch in Michigan’s Democratic Senate Primary
item.description:
Progressive Democrats have fared well in numerous congressional primaries across the country this cycle, winning in urban strongholds like New York City, Denver and Philadelphia. On Tuesday night, Michigan voters in the Democratic Senate primary will test progressives’ statewide appeal in a crucial battleground as they choose between Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate endorsed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official backed by a slew of progressive leaders.

The ideological divides among Michigan Democrats may become apparent as results start coming in after 8 p.m. Eastern. Eight counties, which together made up about two-thirds of the statewide vote in recent Democratic primaries, warrant close attention because they represent critical areas of regional and demographic support for both candidates.

Wayne is the most populous county in the state and will be responsible for around 20 percent of the statewide vote. The candidates’ success there will largely hinge on their appeal to Black voters, particularly in Detroit, the largest city with a Black majority in the United States.

Progressives have sometimes struggled in Democratic primaries in Detroit — Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of Vermont, lost the city by wide margins in his two presidential bids, and Dr. El-Sayed placed third there in his 2018 run for governor.

The Congressional Black Caucus has endorsed Ms. Stevens, who has run ads featuring clips of former President Barack Obama praising her in 2018. (Mr. Obama has not endorsed either candidate.)

Wayne County as a whole is ideologically diverse. In the 2024 presidential primary, several jurisdictions had more voters cast a ballot for “uncommitted” than for President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Many were opposed to Mr. Biden’s support for Israel and its war in Gaza. At the same time, Mr. Biden won 86 percent of the vote in Detroit.

Biden fared poorly in cities with large shares of Arab and Muslim populations.

Sources: Wayne County Clerk, Detroit city clerk.

The New York Times

Several of the areas Mr. Biden lost — including the cities of Dearborn, Dearborn Heights and Hamtramck, which are home to high shares of Arab and Muslim voters — backed Mr. Sanders in 2020 and could favor Dr. El-Sayed, who strongly opposes the United States’ Middle East policies. The nation’s leading pro-Israel PAC has spent about $30 million in support of Ms. Stevens.

The large suburban Detroit counties of Oakland and Macomb are emblematic of two very different kinds of shifts in the Trump era.

Oakland has some of the state’s highest concentrations of high-income, college-educated voters. Historically a Republican stronghold, the county has swung to the left in both state and local races. Ms. Stevens, whose seat covers a large swath of the county, is expected to do well there.

Macomb is decidedly more working class, with white residents without college degrees making up 56 percent of the adult population (in Oakland, it is 35 percent). Mr. Obama won Macomb in 2008 and 2012, but the county then voted for President Trump three elections in a row. Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed are both trying to appeal to voters there, many of whom work in the auto industry. Ms. Stevens has frequently referenced her work on an Obama administration auto rescue task force, while Dr. El-Sayed has secured the backing of the United Auto Workers.

Much like Macomb, Genesee County has trended sharply to the right in the Trump era, with Vice President Kamala Harris winning the county by only four percentage points in 2024 after Mr. Obama won it by nearly 30 percentage points in 2012.

Genesee has consistently supported more moderate candidates in Democratic primaries. Results from Flint, a majority Black city, may be another indicator of how Black voters are leaning.

These counties, home to substantial shares of young voters, are important areas for Dr. El-Sayed. Polls have generally shown him running strongest with voters under 30 — a persistent trend for progressive candidates this cycle.

Washtenaw includes the college towns of Ann Arbor (University of Michigan), where Dr. El-Sayed lives, and Ypsilanti (Eastern Michigan University). Ingham includes East Lansing (Michigan State University), and Kalamazoo includes the city of Kalamazoo (Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo College).

Michigan’s college towns generated large percentages of protest votes against Mr. Biden in the 2024 Democratic primary.

Kent County is among the fastest-growing counties in the state, due in large part to the growth of the Grand Rapids metro area. Kent, which has shifted leftward in recent presidential races, has been a favorable area in the state for progressives: Mr. Sanders won Grand Rapids in both 2016 and 2020.

Representative Hillary Scholten, a Democrat whose district includes much of the Grand Rapids area, has been a sharp critic of Dr. El-Sayed in recent weeks.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Michigan Senate Candidate Haley Stevens
item.description:
Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate fourth-term congresswoman and a favorite of the Democratic establishment, is one of two contenders in her party’s Senate primary in Michigan on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Stevens, 43, of Birmingham, Mich., in suburban Detroit, who is running to replace Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat who is retiring.

1. She is the choice of Democratic leadership in Washington, D.C., and Michigan. Ms. Stevens, who once was a field director for the Michigan Democratic Party, has deep roots in the party. She is not publicly supported by the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm or by Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader. But Mr. Schumer has asked donors to support Ms. Stevens, and sees her as a stronger general election candidate than her left-wing rival, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. She also received endorsements from the state’s popular Democratic governor, Gretchen Whitmer, and from Mr. Peters, the Democrat who is vacating the seat.

2. She is a strong supporter of Israel. Ms. Stevens, running at a moment when Democrats are divided over Israel, has been firm in her position. She supports maintaining unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel. She says she does not believe the Israeli government has carried out a genocide in Gaza. And she calls herself a “proud pro-Israel Democrat.” Her posture has drawn criticism from progressives and support from AIPAC, the hard-line pro-Israel lobbying organization. Dr. El-Sayed, who accuses Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza, has focused on tying her to AIPAC, an organization many Democrats view with deep skepticism. Ms. Stevens has declined to engage with questions about AIPAC’s support. In April, party activists unhappy with her position on Israel booed her at a state party convention. She has maintained that most voters in Michigan are more focused on affordability than foreign policy.

3. Her Michigan accent has been a focus in the race. Ms. Stevens went viral in July after a video circulated on social media showing her at a campaign event. “I’m gonna be doin’ it with a little bit of joy,” she said, punching her hands forward. “A little bit of enthusiasm. A little bit of energy.” And, she continued, punching her right hand into her left palm, “a little bit of stick-it-to-’em! Because that’s the Michigan way!” Her critics mocked the video, but Ms. Stevens seized on the criticism, turning it into a rallying cry. “They’re makin’ fun of Michigan,” she said at an another event. “They’re thinkin’ they’re better than us. And what they don’t know is: I am your voice.”

4. She flipped a House seat in 2018. Ms. Stevens rose to Congress in the midterm elections of President Trump’s first term, winning a suburban Detroit seat that a Republican representative was vacating. Republicans had held the district for decades. Ms. Stevens, who ran on a platform centered on infrastructure and health care access, defeated a business owner. Her victory was part of a year of record gains by women in the House. Another centrist Democrat who flipped a suburban Midwestern seat in 2018, Representative Lauren Underwood of Illinois, has endorsed Ms. Stevens for Senate this year.

5. She has links to Barack Obama (but not his endorsement). Ms. Stevens was an aide on Mr. Obama’s campaign for president in 2008 and later led the Obama administration’s auto task force. In 2018, Mr. Obama endorsed her congressional campaign, and she ran ads that showed him at a rally describing her as a “critical part of my team that helped the American auto industry come roaring back.” During her Senate run, AIPAC’s main super PAC has spent millions to broadcast an ad using the same footage. But Mr. Obama has not weighed in on the Senate race.

item.title: What One Witness Saw Moments Before a Fire Started
item.description:
Paul Child and his grandson were about half a mile from their home outside Spokane, Wash., when they spotted a man standing over a stretch of tall grass and trees near a railroad. The man appeared fidgety and nervous when he saw Mr. Child’s car approaching, Mr. Child said.

Soon after reaching home, Mr. Child heard his daughter call from the backyard, saying she saw smoke nearby.

“I ran out the door,” said Mr. Child, 64, who suspected that the man he had seen had started a fire.

The family called 911 and prepared to evacuate, while Mr. Child drove down the road to warn his neighbors. Within 20 minutes, firefighters and a police officer arrived to a fire that was already out of control.

The authorities said in an affidavit that they had detained a man named Aaron F. Farinacci and asked Mr. Child to confirm whether he was the same man he had seen moments earlier. He did.

The blaze, later named the Old Trails fire, quickly became one of three fast-spreading wildfires in Spokane County that have scorched more than 10,000 acres since last weekend. The fires, which were still active as of Tuesday, have forced some 65,000 people, including the Child family, to evacuate their homes. At least 700 structures have been destroyed in the blazes, but no fatalities have been reported.

When the police detained Mr. Farinacci, 37, on Saturday, the origins of the fires were unknown, according to court records. When Mr. Farinacci was questioned, he denied starting the fire, the affidavit states, and the authorities let him go. By the next day, though, investigators had found that the Old Trails fire was consistent with one started by a lighter or match, and they discovered that it had begun in the same spot where Mr. Child had reported seeing the man.

On Monday, Mr. Farinacci was arrested and charged with one count of first-degree arson, which is punishable by up to life in prison and a $50,000 fine upon conviction. He is being held on a $1 million bond.

Mr. Farinacci made his first court appearance on Tuesday afternoon. A judge kept the bond and said that Mr. Farinacci could not be in possession of any lighters, matches, torches or fire-starting devices if the bond were posted. The judge scheduled an arraignment for Thursday afternoon, when Mr. Farinacci is expected to enter a plea.

Colin Charbonneau, the director of the county public defender’s office, said that he represented Mr. Farinacci during Tuesday’s hearing and that a lawyer in his office would likely be assigned to represent Mr. Farinacci starting Wednesday. He did not comment further on the case.

Mr. Farinacci was carrying waterproof matches and a butane lighter when he was arrested, said Sheriff John Nowels of Spokane County. Court documents show that Mr. Farinacci had been investigated in connection with two fires in Washington last summer, but he was not arrested in either case.

In 2012, Mr. Farinacci was convicted of a felony in Arizona in the death of his father. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter and aggravated assault after initially being charged with first-degree murder, according to court records from Maricopa County.

Records for that case show that Mr. Farinacci, who was 21 years old at the time of the killing, fatally shot his father after an argument in their home. He told investigators that he had not intended to shoot his father and that he had tried to kill himself afterward.

Court records showed a history of mental illness and treatment, but he was declared fit to stand trial. Under a plea deal, the murder charge was dropped, and Mr. Farinacci was released on probation in 2020.

Neither Mr. Farinacci’s mother nor his siblings responded to requests for comment on Tuesday. Nobody answered the door at a Spokane apartment that was listed as Mr. Farinacci’s residence.

At some point after his release on probation, court records show, Mr. Farinacci moved to Washington, where he worked a full-time job and lived with his brother and later with his girlfriend.

On Sunday, Mr. Child returned to his home, which survived the fire. He wondered whether he should have stopped and confronted the man he saw.

“I do second guess myself, whether I could have done something more,” he said. “But it’s good to see there might be accountability.”

Earlier in the week, weather conditions had improved, allowing some evacuees to return. But on Tuesday, the National Weather Service said that smoke from the wildfires had extended into Western Washington and was causing poor air quality. Higher temperatures and drier air forecast for later this week were expected to bring a return to extremely critical fire weather.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Armed Man Arrested at Trump Golf Club Near Los Angeles
item.description:
A California man was arrested at the Trump National Golf Club near Los Angeles over the weekend after he was found with a loaded firearm and seen taking photographs of the property, the authorities said.

The arrest on Sunday came days before President Trump was set to speak at a fund-raiser on Tuesday night at the golf club in Rancho Palos Verdes, an affluent coastal community overlooking the Pacific.

But the man, identified by the authorities as Jeanine John Taele of Downey, Calif., has not been accused of targeting Mr. Trump, and officials have not shared any evidence that his presence was tied to the president’s visit.

Federal agents in plainclothes first reported seeing Mr. Taele, 38, around 3:30 p.m. on Sunday taking photos of the golf course and observing “security-planning activities,” according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department.

Sheriff’s deputies responding to the scene found Mr. Taele carrying a 16-round magazine with hollow-point rounds in his pocket. Inside his car in the parking lot, they found a loaded pistol and another loaded magazine with more hollow-point ammunition.

Mr. Taele was arrested on charges of carrying a concealed firearm and illegal ammunition. Officials also discovered that he was being investigated for robbery in a neighboring city, the sheriff’s department said.

On Tuesday, local detectives assigned to the F.B.I.’s Joint Terrorism Task Force raided Mr. Taele’s home in Downey, a Los Angeles suburb, and recovered a cache of firearms and equipment, including an illegally modified AR-style rifle, a .45-caliber pistol, body armor, high-capacity magazines, ammo and radio equipment.

Detectives also found multiple notebooks containing “concerning statements,” according to the sheriff’s department.

The sheriff’s department said it presented its findings to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office on Tuesday morning. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said that his office was reviewing the evidence.

Mr. Taele remained in custody at the county jail on Tuesday evening. It was unclear if he had legal representation.

In April, a gunman was charged with attempting to assassinate the president after he breached security at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in Washington, where Mr. Trump was in attendance, and exchanged gunfire with law enforcement officials.

In February, a man was sentenced to life in prison for trying to kill the president at another one of his golf clubs, in Florida, in 2024.

And in July 2024, Mr. Trump survived an assassination attempt by a gunman while speaking at campaign rally in Butler, Pa. Mr. Trump was grazed in the ear and an attendee was killed trying to shield his family.

item.title: Michigan Secretary of State Wins Democratic Nomination for Governor
item.description:
Jocelyn Benson, who has cultivated a national profile during two terms as Michigan’s secretary of state, on Tuesday won the Democratic nomination for governor, The Associated Press said.

Ms. Benson is expected to face a competitive general election race as she aims to keep the governorship in Democratic hands. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, the Democratic incumbent, was barred by term limits from seeking re-election.

Michigan is a closely divided swing state that is crucial in presidential races. President Trump won Michigan in 2016 and 2024, but Joseph R. Biden Jr. carried the state in 2020.

Ms. Benson took on a public role in fighting attempts to overturn Mr. Biden’s victory and in defending the accuracy of Michigan’s election results. Since Mr. Trump returned to office, she has fought efforts to force the state to turn over its voter rolls to the federal government.

“Governors are guardrails,” Ms. Benson said at a forum this year hosted by the United Automobile Workers. “If you do not have a governor standing up to the president of the United States and saying, ‘No, I’ll see you in court,’ when you try to break the law,” she added, then “we’re in trouble.”

Michigan will once again be among the most closely watched places in the midterm elections this year, with statewide offices that will administer the next presidential election on the ballot and control of the State Legislature up for grabs. Voters will also choose a new U.S. senator in a race that will help determine control of that chamber.

Ms. Benson, a former law school dean, emerged early on as the front-runner in the Democratic primary for governor. She defeated Sheriff Chris Swanson of Genesee County, who has a large social media following and who spoke at the 2024 Democratic National Convention. Another opponent, Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II, withdrew from the race and is now running for secretary of state.

For months, Michigan had appeared on track for a competitive three-way campaign for governor that would have included Mike Duggan, a former Detroit mayor who left the Democratic Party to run as an independent.

After early success with fund-raising and solid polling, Mr. Duggan withdrew from the race in May after seeing his support slip. His exit was widely seen as benefiting Democrats, who had worried that Mr. Duggan would pull more voters away from Ms. Benson than from her Republican opponent.

item.title: Pastor’s Senate Primary Win Gives Democrats a Ray of Hope in Deep-Red Kansas
item.description:
The Rev. Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Kansas on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, setting up a long-shot challenge to Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, in the general election.

The state has not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in nearly 100 years, and Kansas is not a serious factor in Democrats’ hopes to try to retake the Senate. Democrats would need an extraordinarily strong political environment for the race to even be competitive this year.

But Kansas is not as right-wing as some of its neighbors. Its popular two-term governor, Laura Kelly, is a Democrat, as is one of its four representatives in the U.S. House, Representative Sharice Davids. In 2022, voters resoundingly decided against removing the right to abortion from the State Constitution. And more recently, Kansas farmers were hit hard by the Trump administration’s tariffs.

Mr. Hamilton, for his part, is a credible fund-raiser and a longtime community leader from a populous part of the state. He founded and leads a roughly 24,000-person congregation based in the suburbs of Kansas City, Mo., right across the state line in Kansas.

It’s an area that once favored center-right Republicans, but shifted sharply away from the party during the Trump era, and has since become a crucial source of Democratic turnout.

“In a world that feels more and more divided, our congregation has managed to bring all sorts of people together,” Mr. Hamilton said in his announcement video. “We’re roughly equal parts Republican, Democrat and independent, and we’ve learned to love and appreciate each other precisely because of our differences.”

If that message of moderation plays in the upscale, highly educated suburbs, it could be a different story across the many more conservative pockets of the state. Some voters there tend to look askance at the Kansas City-area suburbs, which they do not regard as “real Kansas.”

Mr. Hamilton, who has been campaigning across the state, will face Mr. Marshall, who comes from a more rural part of Kansas. Mr. Marshall, seeking his second term, has been a strong supporter of President Trump’s.

item.title: Pro-Israel Democrat Fends Off Democratic Socialist’s Comeback Attempt in Missouri
item.description:
Representative Wesley Bell of Missouri, a moderate pro-Israel Democrat, fended off a primary challenge from a former congresswoman and democratic socialist on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, in a loss for the surging socialist movement.

Former Representative Cori Bush, Mr. Bell’s predecessor in the St. Louis district, had hoped to add to the high-profile victories that socialists have notched over Democratic incumbents this year in New York City and Denver.

But Mr. Bell, a former prosecuting attorney and city councilman, held on.

He rose to prominence after the 2014 protests in Ferguson, Mo., which erupted after a white police officer fatally shot Michael Brown, an unarmed Black teenager. In 2018, Mr. Bell ousted the county prosecutor who declined to indict the officer.

In 2024, amid a backlash against progressive politics, Mr. Bell took on Ms. Bush, a member of the so-called Squad — a group of progressive congresswomen of color — and an outspoken critic of Israel’s war in Gaza. He defeated her in the Democratic primary, but since then, Democratic voters have shifted toward Ms. Bush’s tough stance on Israel, which gave her confidence in a potential comeback.

Her bid fell short, however, with Mr. Bell’s deep-pocketed allies spending heavily to stop her, just as they did in 2024. That included more than $2 million from a super PAC associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel group. Mr. Bell’s allies painted Ms. Bush as ineffective and highlighted her vote against former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s infrastructure bill. Mr. Bell will be a heavy favorite in the safely Democratic district in November.

The loss was a setback for democratic socialists, who have gained a foothold in Democratic primaries this year as the party’s voters, fed up with establishment politicians, have shifted toward more liberal positions and the populist, outsider pitches of socialist candidates. In June, socialist candidates ousted three Democratic incumbents, including the chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

The political careers of Mr. Bell and Ms. Bush, who are Black, were both shaped by the Ferguson protests; Ms. Bush was an activist and organizer of them.

item.title: Trump-Backed Lawmaker Wins Kansas Republican Primary for Governor
item.description:
Republican voters selected Ty Masterson, the influential leader of the Kansas Senate, as their nominee for governor on Tuesday, The Associated Press said.

Mr. Masterson, who was endorsed by President Trump, will have perhaps the best chance of any Republican nationally to flip a Democratic-held governorship in November. Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat with a unique political brand, is barred by law from seeking a third term.

Ms. Kelly’s power in Topeka has long been a point of frustration for Republicans, who otherwise dominate Kansas politics. President Trump carried Kansas by 16 percentage points two years ago, and Republicans have used their legislative supermajorities to override Ms. Kelly’s vetoes on a range of conservative priorities.

Even though the party out of power in Washington often performs well in midterm elections, Republicans have high expectations for the open seat in Kansas in November. Democrats, however, have maintained that they have a path to holding the governorship.

Mr. Masterson emerged from a large Republican primary field that included the businessman Philip Sarnecki, Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt and Secretary of State Scott Schwab. Former Gov. Jeff Colyer dropped out of the primary after Mr. Trump endorsed Mr. Masterson.

Though Ms. Schmidt staked out a moderate lane in the primary, the other candidates shared similar views on many policy issues.

Mr. Masterson, Mr. Sarnecki and Mr. Schwab all said they opposed legalizing marijuana. And all of them voiced frustration with the sharp increase in abortions in Kansas since voters declined to change the State Constitution to allow for an abortion ban.

The candidates disagreed about how to regulate data centers and about the merits of a deal that wooed the Kansas City Chiefs, now based in Missouri, to build a new stadium in Kansas.

Mr. Masterson, who was introducing himself to many voters after a career as a Wichita-based legislator, made the president’s support a centerpiece of his campaign.

“As much as I want to make President Trump proud, I want to make you more proud in what I do as a governor,” Mr. Masterson told voters during a recent debate moderated by the Fox affiliate in Kansas City.

Mr. Sarnecki, who gained traction in the race as a newcomer to politics with a long career in private industry, criticized Mr. Masterson as being part of the state’s establishment.

“The contrast could not be more stark,” Mr. Sarnecki said at the debate. “You have the ultimate insider, 20-year career politician, and the outside business leader and job creator.”

Ms. Kelly won her first term eight years ago in another midterm election with Mr. Trump in the White House. But some of the political dynamics that helped lift her to that victory, including unpopular tax policies passed by Republicans and a Republican nominee whom many voters found unpalatable, might not be major factors in this year’s race.

Though not a household name in much of the state, Mr. Masterson has amassed political power during nearly two decades in the Kansas Capitol. During his tenure as president of the State Senate, lawmakers overrode Ms. Kelly’s vetoes of dozens of bills, including ones that placed restrictions on transgender people, overhauled election procedures and limited officials’ ability to impose restrictions during public health emergencies.

But with Ms. Kelly in office, Mr. Masterson’s power was sometimes limited. Though he and other legislative Republicans wanted to redraw the state’s congressional map last year, he would have needed near-unanimous Republican support to overcome a veto from the governor. That plan unraveled when several Republicans voiced opposition, leaving in place a single Democratic-leaning U.S. House district.

item.title: Kansas Rejects Measure to Elect Its State Supreme Court Justices
item.description:
Kansas voters on Tuesday rejected a ballot measure that would have required state Supreme Court justices to be popularly elected rather than appointed by the governor, dealing another setback to Republican lawmakers trying to overturn a decision that established a constitutional right to abortion.

That ruling in 2019 has preserved Kansas as a significant abortion provider for women in a wide swath of middle-American states that banned abortion after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.

The Republican-controlled Legislature put the amendment on Tuesday’s ballot, arguing that the court had repeatedly failed to represent the will of the state’s voters. Lawmakers disagreed with other court rulings, including one requiring the Legislature to spend more on public schools.

But Republican leaders made clear to anti-abortion groups that the measure was mainly aimed at abortion.

The Legislature had tried and failed before to get voters to reverse the court ruling, putting an amendment on the ballot in August 2022 that would have amended the constitution to say there was no right to abortion. The vote came six weeks after the reversal of Roe, and 59 percent of Kansas voters rejected the amendment.

That vote inspired abortion rights supporters in a dozen other states to pass ballot measures establishing or affirming a constitutional right to abortion.

Both opponents and supporters of the ballot measure defeated on Tuesday had argued that its passage would inspire Republican-controlled legislatures in other states to remake appointed courts that have blocked bans on abortion and gender care, and upheld nonpartisan redistricting commissions.

With conservatives dominating the U.S. Supreme Court, groups that support abortion and L.G.B.T.Q. rights in particular have turned to state supreme courts to establish those rights in their constitutions.

Kansas is one of 21 states with an assisted appointment system. The governor — since 2019, a Democrat and a supporter of abortion — selects justices from a list put forward by a nine-member nominating commission. The governor appoints four members of the commission and the state’s lawyers elect five. New justices face a retention election after their first year and every six years after that.

item.title: Missouri Voters Reject Measure to Limit Their Ballot Box Powers
item.description:
Missouri voters on Tuesday rejected an attempt by the Republican-controlled Legislature to make it harder to pass citizen-sponsored amendments to the state’s constitution, preserving a tool that voters across the country have relied on to pass laws their legislatures would not.

The Legislature, like others across the country, had pushed back after voters approved citizen-sponsored amendments that expanded Medicaid, legalized marijuana and sports betting, established a right to abortion, raised the minimum wage and required paid sick leave.

The measure would have amended the state’s constitution to require a majority in each of the state’s eight congressional districts, rather than a simple majority statewide, to pass citizen-sponsored amendments. That would have been the highest threshold in any of the 18 states that allow citizen groups to place constitutional amendments on the ballot.

Opponents of the measure, including a state real estate association and abortion rights groups, said that under the measure, an amendment could win the support of 95 percent of the state’s voters but still fail, based on recent voter tallies. None of the four amendments Missouri voters have passed since 2020 have won in all congressional districts.

The higher threshold would not have applied to amendments placed on the ballot by the Legislature; those would have continued to require a simple majority to pass.

The amendment was the latest of the Legislature’s attempts to thwart citizen-sponsored ballot initiatives. After the amendment on the minimum wage and sick leave passed, the Legislature passed a law striking the sick leave provisions. It has placed an amendment on the ballot in November that would repeal a citizen-led initiative from 2024 that established a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, including abortion. That measure passed with 52 percent of the vote, and the vote in November is expected to be close.

Missouri has a long tradition of citizen-sponsored ballot initiatives dating back to the early 20th century. Those initiatives include several unsuccessful attempts at prohibition before a federal ban on alcohol took effect, and a successful effort in 1976 to repeal constitutional language that allowed the legislature to require segregated schools, 22 years after Brown v. Board of Education.

item.title: Arizona’s Democratic Governor Set to Pick a Republican Running Mate
item.description:
Gov. Katie Hobbs of Arizona, a vulnerable Democrat running for re-election, plans to tap a longtime Republican and former mayor of a Phoenix suburb to serve as her running mate, according to two people familiar with the decision.

John Giles, a former mayor of Mesa, Ariz., is expected to be announced in the coming days as Ms. Hobbs’s lieutenant governor nominee. Neither Ms. Hobbs nor her campaign would confirm the choice, and nothing is final until an announcement.

But the apparent pick is a nod to bipartisanship in a campaign that will pit Ms. Hobbs, a low-key Democrat, against Representative Andy Biggs, a fiercely partisan Republican with President Trump’s endorsement.

Ms. Hobbs’s narrow victory four years ago was secured with the backing of moderate Republicans and independent voters who have recoiled against hard-line Republican nominees in each of the last two election cycles.

Reached at his home in Mesa, Mr. Giles would not confirm or deny that he had joined the ticket, but a person close to the campaign and another close to Mr. Giles said the choice had been made.

Arizonans for the first time this November will elect a lieutenant governor running on the same ticket as the governor, thanks to a 2022 ballot measure that created the lieutenant governor position.

Calli Jones, a spokeswoman for the Arizona secretary of state’s office, said the office told all governor candidates last Friday that their lieutenant governor picks must be submitted by Aug. 7 to ensure the office has enough time to print their names on the November ballot.

Arizona has emerged as a critical swing state since President Trump carried it in 2016, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. won it in 2020, and Mr. Trump won it back in 2024. Ms. Hobbs defeated Kari Lake, a close Trump ally, by less than a percentage point in 2022, the same year another hard-right ally of the president’s, Blake Masters, lost his Senate bid. Ms. Lake lost her own Senate bid in 2024.

Mr. Biggs, a member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, will again try to expand an appeal to the state’s Trump base into a broader winning coalition. Last week, Mr. Biggs announced his own lieutenant governor pick, Sine Kerr, a former state lawmaker, dairy farmer and strong conservative.

A spokesman for Ms. Hobbs’s campaign, Michael Beyer, said only that the campaign had held multiple events with Mr. Giles “since he became the first endorsement in our Arizona Over Party coalition,” a cohort of dozens of Republicans and independents backing the governor’s re-election.

Mr. Giles, who endorsed Kamala Harris two years ago, told The New York Times last year that he had discussed the lieutenant governor role with Ms. Hobbs in 2024. He rebuffed her initial overtures, as did Jimmy McCain, the son of longtime Senator John McCain of Arizona, according to three people familiar with the outreach to Mr. Giles and Mr. McCain.

Last year, Mr. Giles told The Times that he was skeptical of how much the selection of a moderate Republican like himself would help Ms. Hobbs broaden her appeal if she faced Karrin Taylor Robson, another moderate Republican who was at the time running for governor. But Ms. Taylor Robson dropped out of the Republican primary in February after polling far behind Mr. Biggs.

A longtime critic of Mr. Trump, Mr. Giles spoke at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago in 2024, urging moderates to vote for Ms. Harris and saying he felt “more at home here than in today’s Republican Party.” He is one of many members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints who have drifted away from the Republican Party in the Trump era.

Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting.

item.title: Lawmaker Who Wants Data Center Pause Wins Kansas Democratic Primary
item.description:
Kansas Democrats have defied political gravity for eight years by holding the governor’s office in one of the country’s most reliably Republican states.

On Tuesday, primary voters selected State Senator Cindy Holscher as the candidate to try to keep that seat in Democratic hands, according to The Associated Press. Ms. Holscher defeated a fellow lawmaker, State Senator Ethan Corson, who was backed by the outgoing Democratic governor, Laura Kelly. Mayor Curt Skoog of Overland Park also sought the nomination.

The race became a test of what sort of candidate Democratic voters prefer in what is expected to be a challenging general election race: a more moderate candidate like Mr. Corson with endorsements from party leaders or an outspoken populist like Ms. Holscher, who spoke out against data centers and the political establishment.

Even in a national political environment that could favor Democrats, Republicans see the Kansas governorship as among their best opportunities for flipping a seat. President Trump carried Kansas by 16 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans hold supermajorities in the State Legislature. Voters in the Republican primary for governor nominated Ty Masterson, the president of the Kansas Senate and the recipient of Mr. Trump’s endorsement, according to The A.P.

Ms. Holscher, who is from suburban Kansas City, sought out a lane to Mr. Corson’s political left and made inroads with some of the state’s progressive voters. She emphasized her role in unwinding former Gov. Sam Brownback’s tax policies and called for a moratorium on data centers. She also spoke against a final deal to lure the Kansas City Chiefs across the state line from Missouri.

Ms. Holscher presented an implicit critique of Ms. Kelly’s stewardship of Kansas, referring to Mr. Corson as part of a political establishment that was too cozy with corporations and out of touch with the party’s voters.

“We have in front of us the ability to hire someone essentially who will work for the working people of Kansas,” Ms. Holscher said at a recent debate hosted by PBS Kansas, “or hire someone who will take you down the path of the status quo and continue working for the establishment.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Corson, who represents a safely Democratic district in suburban Kansas City, positioned himself as the heir to the Kelly political coalition.

Governor Kelly, who has won far more votes than other Democrats in conservative rural counties, filmed a commercial supporting Mr. Corson as her preferred successor. And Mr. Corson described himself as someone who could appeal to a range of voters, not just loyal Democrats.

“What Kansas Democrats should be thinking about is who can win this race in November,” Mr. Corson said at the PBS debate.

Ms. Kelly, herself a former state senator who emerged from a competitive primary, offers proof that Democrats can sometimes win in Kansas — even though Republicans have carried it in every presidential election since the 1960s.

In 2018, Ms. Kelly defeated Kris W. Kobach, now the state attorney general, by riding a wave of voter discontent with Republican tax policies and Mr. Kobach’s brash political style. Four years later, Ms. Kelly won re-election in a national environment that was less favorable to Democrats by branding herself as the “middle-of-the-road” candidate.

Kansas is among four Midwestern states — along with Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin — where Democrats flipped governorships in 2018, and where the party is seeking to maintain control this year. Of those, all but Illinois are expected to be competitive, but Kansas is considered to be Democrats’ most difficult electoral fight.

Mr. Masterson, who won a competitive primary, will run on the president’s endorsement and a record of leading a Republican supermajority in the Senate to override Ms. Kelly’s vetoes on a range of conservative priorities, including restricting official recognition of transgender identity and overhauling election laws.

Still, Democrats are hopeful that Ms. Kelly’s record and Kansas voters’ independent streak could help them hold onto the governor’s office in November. The state’s most populous county, Johnson County in suburban Kansas City, has shifted dramatically toward Democrats during the Trump era, and Kansas voters rejected an effort in 2022 to change the State Constitution to allow for a ban on abortion. Kansas Democrats have historically performed better in midterm elections than in presidential years, with several Democratic governors elected in recent decades.

Democrats hope to retain their single seat in the Kansas congressional delegation in November. Though Republicans sought to redraw U.S. House district lines last year, Ms. Kelly’s expected veto meant that almost every Republican lawmaker would have had to agree to enact a new map. Several Republicans scuttled the plan, leaving in place a left-leaning district in the Kansas City area that is held by Representative Sharice Davids, a Democrat.

item.title: Trump-Backed Lawmaker Wins Republican Nomination for Michigan Governor
item.description:
Representative John James, a two-term congressman from suburban Detroit, on Tuesday won the Republican nomination for governor of Michigan, The Associated Press said.

Mr. James, who was endorsed by President Trump, is expected to face a competitive general election race as Republicans seek to flip Michigan’s governorship. He will face Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who won the Democratic primary on Tuesday, according to The A.P. The Democratic incumbent, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, was ineligible to seek re-election because of term limits.

Mr. James is familiar to Michigan voters, having twice appeared on statewide ballots in recent years. He lost U.S. Senate races in 2018 and in 2020 before winning election to the U.S. House in a swing district in 2022.

Mr. James defeated Perry Johnson, a businessman who self-funded his campaign and called for eliminating the state income tax. On the campaign trail, Mr. James emphasized his military service and his endorsement from Mr. Trump. He would become Michigan’s first Black governor if he wins in November.

As governor, Mr. James said, he would seek to increase transparency in state government by requiring more financial disclosures from government officials and by eliminating exemptions in open records laws.

Michigan is an evenly divided swing state that is crucial in presidential races. President Trump won Michigan in 2016 and 2024, but Joseph R. Biden Jr. carried the state in 2020.

The state will once again be among the most closely watched places in the midterm elections this year, with offices that will administer the next presidential election on the ballot and control of the Michigan Legislature on the line. Voters will also elect a new U.S. senator in a race that could determine which party controls that chamber.

The race for governor will present voters with two established political figures with starkly different views of the country under Mr. Trump.

Ms. Benson, a two-term secretary of state, took on a public role in fighting attempts to overturn Mr. Biden’s victory in 2020 and in defending the accuracy of Michigan’s election results.

Since Mr. Trump returned to office, she has fought efforts to force the state to turn over its voter rolls to the federal government and has vowed to defend Michigan from what she describes as threats to democracy.

Mr. James has echoed Mr. Trump’s claims that the 2020 election was “rigged” and has criticized Ms. Whitmer’s administration of Michigan, saying the state is “on fire.”

“We have higher taxes, we have high electricity bills, our kids can’t read, and criminals are back on the street,” Mr. James said in a recent debate hosted by WJBK-TV. “But we can fix that.”
